speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps hon. members would welcome at this time a brief statement as to the extent of the remaining legislative program which the government proposes to submit for the consideration of parliament before the end of the session. Fortunately there is not much left, but in addition to the bills and resolutions now appearing on the order paper and the two resolutions of which notice appears in Votes and Proceedings of yesterday, there are the several measures which have been referred to the committees. These include the Treaty of Peace (Japan) Act, the amendment to the Canada Grain Act, the amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act, the amendment to the Veterans Benefit Act, the amendment to the Veterans Insurance Act and the redistribution legislation. It is expected that these measures will be reported back to the house in due course and will be required to be dealt with.
There are three measures which were before the Senate, one of which has just been passed by that house. If the two remaining measures are disposed of in that place in time they will be sent here for consideration. These are the Criminal Code revision and the amendment to the Food and Drugs Act.
The government expects within the next few days to give notice of a bill dealing with the Belleville harbour commissioners and there will be the usual annual bill respecting Canadian National finances. It is hoped and expected that at an early date we will have the final polishing up given to a bill which has been under consideration for some time dealing with currency, the mint and the exchange fund. There may also be
a resolution to approve of an agreement for the promotion of safety on the great lakes and there will probably be introduced in the Senate a bill dealing with trade-marks. It is not intended that that bill shall go beyond the committee stage in that house at this session. It is being introduced, as the Bankruptcy Act and the Income Tax Act were introduced, so that it may get publicity and so that during the recess of parliament interested parties may make such representations, or prepare themselves to make such representations, as they may see fit at another session.
We have another bill that has been ready for some time to amend the Eastern Rocky Mountain Forest Conservation Act but it cannot be introduced until the revised contract with the government of Alberta has been completed. If that is completed in time to make it convenient without rushing matters here to introduce the confirmatory legislation that will be done. So far as I know there is nothing else in contemplation, and that will complete the whole program.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question with particular reference to one matter to which he referred, the revision of the Criminal Code. The law societies have had a general opportunity afforded by the Minister of Justice to examine the measure but in view of its amplitude and the fact that the law societies have not had a full opportunity to examine its terms, and having several letters on my desk with regard to the various provisions, I should like to inquire whether the Prime Minister will consider allowing that measure to stand over. After all, no real harm would be done by allowing it to stand over until the next session so that every representation consistent with the principles of justice embodied in the Criminal Code may be made. I make that suggestion because I feel that so important a piece of work as the amendments to the Criminal Code certainly should not be rushed through the house until the law societies and others interested have had the fullest opportunity to study the matter and if necessary make further representations in addition to those they have already made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
There has never been any intention to rush it through the house. It is a measure which is not controversial in party

Business of the House political terms. It is a measure that is being devised for the better administration of the criminal law for the whole Canadian public. We fully appreciate that it has to receive the most careful consideration. We are under the impression that the law societies and others outside parliament have had a full opportunity to make their views known. There are many lawyers in this house, as there are in the other place, and I am sure that every one of them will feel a personal responsibility to give due consideration to all the sections of the measure amending the Criminal Code.
I think it would not be advisable to try to deal with it in this house if it did not reach us at least a fortnight before the approximate date for prorogation of parliament. It is not something which has to be passed at this session. However, it has been delayed inevitably for a long time and we would not care to delay it any longer than is reasonably necessary to make it acceptable as a piece of legislation having had the most careful consideration possible from those who will be responsible for its enactment. We had already given the matter consideration and had come to the conclusion that unless it reached this house at least a fortnight before the target date for prorogation it would not be proper to try to have it considered in a hurry.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I would point out that there may be a consideration that should be borne in mind in that respect. Already, as the Prime Minister knows, some representations have been made that the legislation should stand over in order to provide a further opportunity for discussion. To some extent what members of the house will do in the meantime will depend on whether the legislation is or is not going to be proceeded with. I believe that a number of members will perhaps wish to answer the communications they have received with some knowledge whether it is or is not proposed to proceed with the legislation. Therefore without asking that a definite statement be made today, I wish the Prime Minister would consider that feature of the subject because many of us would probably feel that we would simply answer the letters we have received by saying that it is the intention of the government to permit further consideration, if that is the intention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
We know of no reason, other than the time required to give the matter careful study in the house, that would justify retarding the coming into force of the legislation, but it may very well be that the kind of consideration that it should be given by members of the house will make it

undesirable to have it completed at this session. I think the general public would naturally wish to have it come into force in proper form just as soon as that task can be accomplished, and I would not like to make any commitment to other bodies that it would be delayed for any other reason than that members of parliament would not have been satisfied in the meantime that they had had all the information that might be of benefit to them in helping them to discharge their responsibility.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: One of the questions I had intended to direct to the Prime Minister has already been put by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Perhaps I might be permitted to say that we support the suggestion that the Criminal Code amending bill should stand over until next session, for the reason suggested by the Prime Minister as well as for other reasons. The other question I wish to ask is in two parts. Will there be introduced at this session the legislation indicated in the speech from the throne respecting the Canadian Citizenship Act, and will there also be introduced at this session the legislation to amend the Government Annuities Act which we had before us at the last session of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
With respect to the
Canadian Citizenship Act, at the present time it is not contemplated that it will be dealt with at this session. It has always been contemplated that that would depend upon what was done with the Immigration Act. It was felt that if the Immigration Act as proposed were adopted in exactly that form it might be desirable to have concurrent amendments made to the Canadian Citizenship Act. However, it is not now intended to bring them forward at this session because even when the Immigration Act is enacted it will be provided that it is not to come into force until proclaimed, and it will not be possible to proclaim it at once because it will require some preliminary organization changes before it is proclaimed.
With respect to the annuities act and two or three others mentioned in the speech from the throne, we have not yet got them in the shape that we would wish to have them to recommend them to parliament, and we do not expect to have them in shape to enable us to recommend them to parliament at this session.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister one other question with regard to the Criminal Code? How does the government propose that this measure shall be handled if and when it does come to the house? Is it

intended that it should be considered in committee of the whole after second reading or referred to some select committee after second reading?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: That point has not been decided. It is a matter in which it is felt that all members of the house of course are interested, but I think those members of the house who are not of the legal fraternity will look to their confreres of the legal fraternity to take the principal part in discharging the responsibility of getting the revised code in proper shape. No decision has been arrived at as to whether the most convenient form would be the committee of the whole or a special committee made up principally of the lawyer members of the house. My own view would be that it would probably take less time and might meet with the approval of the non-lawyer members of the house to have it referred to a committee of lawyers. I would not want to press that on the house if other members felt that they also wanted to take part in the detailed examination of the various clauses of the bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: You have got to have some common sense in it.

On the 4th of June, the day before yesterday, the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) asked a question about the situation in South Korea. I had the answer yesterday but the hon. member was not in his seat at the time the orders of the day were called. Though he has not yet come in this afternoon I think I should make a short answer so as not to leave the impression that I have not given his question the consideration it deserved.
Previous to the visit of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to New York yesterday and the day before, our permanent delegate to the United Nations, on instructions from Ottawa, had expressed to the Secretary General of the United Nations our concern over the situation in South Korea. Mr. Speaker, referring to questions at pages 2787 and 2788 of Hansard of Monday last, June 2, the answers or the supposed answers which appear in Hansard are not the same as those that I have received. They pertain to the Canadian National Railways and on each answer, which bears the signature of the deputy minister of transport, there is:
Answer: The Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
That appears on both answers. However, it does not appear on Hansard and that makes all the difference in the world, because the answers which I hold in my hand are typewritten and have just been conveyed to the House of Commons by the minister and not given by him. They are not the minister's answers; they are the answers of the railway.
I would ask the minister if I am right in that respect-and I have a second question to ask him.

If the answer had been given by the railway and conveyed by the minister to the house, are the answers from the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways or are they answers from the management?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house is familiar with the practice in so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. Questions when asked are put on the order paper and submitted by the officials of the Department of Transport to the officials of the Canadian National Railways, and the answers given by the railway officials to the questions are the answers which are tabled in this house. Normally it is stated in the answer that the Canadian National Railways advise as follows:
And the answers follow, 1, 2, 3.
That is the practice, but if it has been omitted-and I note that it has in the questions to which my hon. friend refers at pages 2787 and 2788 of Hansard-I have no objection to that being inserted, but it is a matter for the house to determine and not for me.
Dealing with the questions of my hon. friend, I think what I have said so far answers his first question. The second question would be answered by the fact that these are not the answers of the board of directors. Questions are not sent to the board of directors, they are sent to the officers of the Canadian National Railways with whom our officers are in contact. The replies submitted by them are the replies which are given by myself to the house.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I thank the minister for his fair answer which will permit me to use proper language with regard to the Canadian National Railways people in due course- language that I would never use toward him.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before we go on with item 259, may I ask a question about the statement which the minister put on the record just at the moment of adjournment last night. In comparing the statement of the actual expenditures, item by item, which the minister tabled late last night with the estimates of 1951-52, I notice that in many instances the expenditures exceeded the estimates. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The further supplementaries are not included. Those items are covered by further supplementaries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I then make this observation on this volume of estimates. I suppose the same thing will apply to all departments, and not just the Department of National Health and Welfare. When figures are shown as being the estimates for the year 1951-52 for comparison with the year 1952-53, we are given apparently only the original or main estimates for the year 1951-52, and the supplementary estimates or further supplementary estimates are not included in those figures. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I had asked a question of the minister in regard to No. 259. Will he tell us how many lepers there are at the two establishments, the one at Bentinck island in British Columbia and the other at Tracadie in New Brunswick.

speechtext: I believe that this item was referred to some years ago, and questions were asked about the necessity of maintaining a place for the treatment of lepers. I hear that there are eight such people in British Columbia now, and a year ago there was one. This difficulty in Korea, and the constant traffic back and forth across the Pacific, may very well expose us to the dangers of this sort of disease. I believe the minister should be commended for maintaining an institution where patients may be treated, and also maintaining a very close observation of persons landing on these shores from the Pacific. I believe it is very much better for the nation to save money by preventive measures, instead of spending money after there has been an occurrence of this and other diseases in many places.

260.	Immigration and medical services, $1,198,360.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This is a large item that
relates to the immigration medical services, and shows some increase over last year. In referring to the details on page 322, I notice that the number of medical officers is being increased from 28 to 47. There is also a substantial increase in the number of housemaids. There is a provision for 24 assistants, who are new. I wonder if the minister would

Supply-Health and Welfare review the situation in regard to the maintenance of these services, particularly in the light of immigration policy outlined to us, and give us the duties and qualifications of the various persons who are being added to the staff in these respective capacities.
I would ask the minister also to indicate what will be the effect, if any, on the administration of the immigration medical services, following the adoption of the new Immigration Act which has been introduced in the house? Will he tell us something about the plans of the department in regard to locating medical examiners abroad, and particularly if there are any changes in contemplation. I would ask him to tell us something, in general, about the health of immigrants. The minister is aware that early in March the minister of health for Ontario reported with some regret that during the last four years more than 70,000 days of treatment had been provided for displaced persons in Ontario, at a cost to the province of considerably more than $200,000. He mentioned that the tuberculosis rate was two and a half times that of Canadians, and indicates that these immigrants were apparently more susceptible than Canadians to arthritis and other diseases. Will the minister make a statement covering the points I have mentioned?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I was going to ask several questions along the lines of those asked by the member for Eglinton. There is one particular point I cannot understand and that is that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration told us there would be 30,000 to 40,000 less immigrants this year than we had last year, so why should we have to spend $307,000 more examining them with an additional staff of 40 people? The two things do not seem to jibe, so would the minister give an explanation?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I wanted to ask the minister if this item pays for any of the doctors and nurses on our immigration staff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Entirely. I take it that there are no other questions on this item, so I shall deal with them now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have some other detailed questions to ask.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then I suggest that the hon. member do it now, and I shall deal with them all at once.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would prefer to have a general answer, and then ask the detailed questions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
First of all, with regard to the last question. The entire services of
(Mr. Fleming.]

the examination staff are under this vote. As the committee will realize, we service the immigration department as we service other departments of government in other ways. While there is not complete centralization of medical services, an effort is made, in so far as it is possible, and in the light of all conditions, to make the Department of National Health and Welfare provide the medical services for those departments of government requiring them.
Our budget is determined, not by our own departmental program, but by the requirements that follow the program of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration itself. There has been an increase to the extent of 19 medical officers, together with consequential staff that has to be employed, not only abroad, but for the functions they exercise at our hospitals and our centres at Gander, Harmon field, Sydney, Halifax, Moncton, Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver and so on. I do not know that anything arises in which we are concerned in the proposed citizenship bill, or in the amendments to the act to which the hon. member has referred. I am not aware of anything that would affect us consequentially. However, I may not have fully understood the hon. member's point.
It is true that the minister of health in Ontario did point to the great danger, and properly so, in his position of minister of health in that province. But I can assure my hon. friend, as did my parliamentary assistant when he replied on March 7 to a question asked in the house along the same lines. His answer is reported at page 203 of Hansard. I can assure my hon. friend that the greatest care is taken in the examination of proposed immigrants.
In respect of certain persons, such as epileptics, mental cases, tubercular cases and those affected with trachoma, as well as venereal disease, not only are the proposed immigrants examined themselves, but the members of their families are also examined. Then, for more than two and a half years there has been the requirement of X-rays from the proposed immigrant in the country of origin. The greatest care is taken in the examination of the proposed immigrants. In many instances there is re-examination. This does not happen in every case; but where for some reason or another an immigrant may be considered as possibly undesirable, there is re-examination here at the point of disembarkation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Would the minister indicate whether in the past year the proportion of immigrants medically examined abroad, before beginning their journey to Canada, has increased. I notice in the last annual

report of the department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951, at page 69 there is the following statement:
During the year a total of 136,755 immigrants were medically examined abroad and 77,348 on arrival in Canada. Of the numbers examined 42,445 were from the British Isles, 92,076 from Europe and 2,234 from the orient.
Has there been any increase in the percentage of those examined abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, a very considerable
increase, over 100 per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is what we would expect from the increased appropriation last year, and the increase still being provided. Would the minister deal more specifically with my inquiry in regard to assistants? As will be seen in the details at page 323 provision is made for 24 assistants. I have asked about their duties and qualifications, and I am also curious to know about the addition of 22 housemaids, in the particulars as they are shown at page 322.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are opening our hospital at Rockhead, we have our hospital in the west, and our Park Savard hospital. If there are more immigrants, that means that more staff is necessary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I gathered from what the minister said that these personnel, the assistants and housemaids, are located in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, and some outside. For instance we are opening a new office in Oslo and the doctors have to have assistants there. We have some, too, in London and in the Paris office. But this staff is the staff thought to be necessary in the light of the policy of the immigration branch.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are they assistants-because that is what they are called in the details?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, that is what they are.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are they medical assistants to the doctors?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: X-ray operators, clerks, typists and that sort of assistant.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In other words it includes all kinds of staff?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am not clear on what the minister has said. If we are to have 40,000 less immigrants this year than we had last year-and I think that was what the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration announced a few weeks ago-why do we need this staff?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I can only say that if we are going to have less we will not require the same staff. All we are doing is to service
Supply-Health and Welfare another department of government. If the staff is not required it will not be utilized.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: But if the minister would turn to page 323 he would see there an estimate for hospital materials and supplies, in which there is an increase of $60,000. If there are to be fewer immigrants, why do we have this increase?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend may be assured that if we do not need the staff and do not need the material or cannot find adequate places to use it, we will not order it. But our staff is predicated upon the requirements to service the needs of the department. If the government should decide upon a different policy for this service, then we will have to cut our cloth accordingly. But we have to provide the equipment and the commodities used to give the kind of examination that the hon. member for Eglinton urged, and properly so, should be maintained.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I understand that; but let me say this, that if our immigration policy has been cut, then these estimates should be cut.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think the hon. member fails to realize that if he will compare the estimates this year with the main and supplementary estimates for last year he will find that they do not take into account last year's further supplementary estimates of $508,000. If these are taken into consideration, then the present estimates will appear as a decrease of $200,000. The blue book makes no reference to last year's further supplementary estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I notice that the item for allowances at page 323 is an increase from $53,184 to $127,536. What is the reason for this?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Those allowances are for our officers and personnel abroad, in accordance with the general policy of the government regarding officers in all departments who serve outside Canada and who, in view of special conditions attaching to residence outside the country, are provided for in this way.

261.	Sick mariners treatment services, $588,129.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What class of mariners is affected? Are these persons in the service of the government, or does the item apply to any sailor in private enterprise? I know of two sailors-or mariners, as we call them- who have been sick all winter down home, and have not received treatment of any kind. They have had no service from the department, so far as I am aware.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The treatment that is provided is for sailors for whom fees are paid.

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This is a matter with which I first became familiar just a short time ago. I understand that this is in the nature of a medical insurance scheme, and the people who come under it are the members of the crew of any ship which pays a fee, and I think it is two cents per ton gross tonnage, every time it comes into port. The chief beneficiaries are fishermen, particularly along the Atlantic coast, and I understand there is a hospital, or there are hospitals, operated by this branch. Can the minister tell us where the hospitals are operated and how many are operated and whether they are operated continuously?
We are asked here to vote $588,000 when, as a matter of fact, the amount of money which will actually be required is about $250,000 less than that. The amount collected from the fishermen and from ships of various sorts that come in, as I understand it, makes up the revenue which, in the details on page 324, was $240,000 last year and is estimated at $250,000 this year. It would seem to me that this thing should be set up in such a way that we would be voting the actual amount of money required rather than the total amount of money which is spent.
I presume that the revenue collected goes into the consolidated revenue fund, but as for showing what the actual position is of this medical insurance scheme for fishermen and mariners, which I think is a good thing, we should be voting the actual amount which is required rather than the total expenditures made, because I do not think this gives us the true picture.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Well, as my hon. friend knows, there is a deficit in this. Theoretically this is a revenue bearing scheme, but the revenue does not take care of the positive obligations. As the deputy minister of health explained the other day before one of the committees- perhaps my hon. friend was a member of the committee-there is a problem and my hon. friend may be familiar with it. I feel strongly that you could make a pretty strong case for increasing the fees so as to make a greater equality between obligations incurred and moneys received by way of revenue. But it is thought that if that were done it would mean that a great many fishermen on the Atlantic coast would be denied medical services.
As to the accounting problem that my hon. friend has mentioned, I will make note of it, and see that it is given further consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is not an accounting problem. I do not think it is an accounting problem; I think it is a matter of the picture which is presented through the estimates to parliament and to the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes. With regard to the question as to where the hospitals are, marine hospitals are operated at Sydney and Lunenburg, Nova Scotia; sick mariners' clinics at the ports of Vancouver, Montreal, Quebec, Saint John, and Halifax, will continue to be operated as usual, a new sick mariners' clinic is planned for Victoria, British Columbia, and is expected to provide increased facilities for the care of out-patients. Elsewhere in the province in which the act operates, the various port physicians are paid either on a fee or part-time salary basis as conditions warrant, and we have not contemplated any essential changes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In connection with what the minister said in regard to increasing the fees, the information that we got in the committee, to which he referred, was that the fees have been constant since 1868. I think there has been no increase in the fees since that time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Until not very long ago the revenue taken in from these fees was equal to the expenditures incurred. I think in all the time of operation the total deficit to date is only around a million dollars, and most of that, I presume, has been incurred in the last few years when hospital costs and so forth have gone up so extensively. I would think that possibly some small increase in that rate might make the scheme more or less self-liquidating again without, as the minister expressed it, making it impossible for the fishermen to take advantage of it.
I was rather surprised at the list of hospitals that the minister gave because the total amount of expenditure, including revenue, is only $588,000, and I am quite sure it would not be possible to run all these hospitals on that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: These hospitals are not used exclusively by us for that one single purpose. My hon. friend asked at what places or at what hospitals were we giving the service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I asked at what places you were operating hospitals under this particular item, and I think the minister gave most of the hospitals that are operated not only under this branch but under various other departments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The Sydney hospital is an Indian hospital in the main now, but we do treat sick mariners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Perhaps the minister can tell us what hospitals are operated by this branch.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Sydney and Lunenburg are the only ones exclusively for this purpose. At our Park Savard hospital in Quebec, which was originally entirely used for immigration

purposes, we found it was too big for that and some years ago we converted it into an Indian hospital. We have not only Indians in that hospital; we actually lease some space incidentally to veterans affairs because of the existing current shortage of hospital space for veterans in Quebec city. At Rockhead we also treat Indians as well as sick mariners.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: One other question on this, Mr. Chairman. What is the reason that mariners or fishermen are not eligible beyond the borders of Ontario and Quebec? In other words, all the ones on the St. Lawrence river from that point westward on the great lakes are not eligible.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Well, my hon. friend has touched a problem that has concerned me right from the time I became the minister of this department, and every other minister, I am sure, who has been in charge of this department. This particular service developed in the first instance out of a convention between various member states to protect the health of sick mariners travelling from the home country. It was confirmed by the league of nations, but it had been done before that. But long before the present time, because the maritime provinces and the province of British Columbia are maritime provinces traditionally, there was a difficulty sometimes in differentiating between sailors who are operating from one port in the country to a port in another country. Then there developed the difficulty that sometimes a ship travelling let us say from Quebec to Cherbourg would stop at Saint John or Halifax, two ports in our own country, and men would be sick, and the question arose: Are you going to continue treatment of these people? They would have got this treatment if they had gone to France. That policy developed, and we then had demands for treatment of sailors on the great lakes. The same policy has been urged. Well, we have had to resist that, and I think properly so, because people operating in inland waters have the same facilities of medical attention that any other citizen has in that province, and yet there is the anomaly in the case of some individuals. I can say no more than to state that the anomaly does exist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Some reference has been made to this vote being of importance to fishermen on the Atlantic coast, but I think the minister will agree with me when I say that it applies only to boats of a certain tonnage and fishermen working on boats below that would receive no benefit whatsoever.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is not every fisherman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Hand liners and fishermen working with motor boats off the maritime
Supply-Health and Welfare coast would receive no benefit whatsoever. Benefits would be received only by those operating bankers and going out to sea with boats of larger tonnage. Did the minister say that there was a hospital at Lunenburg and Sydney operated by the department? I notice that only one matron is mentioned in the details.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How many contribute?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

Laboratory of hygiene-
264. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $424,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There is an item in the details on page 327 of $400,000 covering the construction of a virus laboratory. Where is this laboratory to be located and what is its direct purpose?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is proposed to locate this laboratory at Tunney's Pasture in the west end of Ottawa and I may say that it is greatly needed and has been long overdue as the present quarters of the virus section are wholly inadequate. The new laboratory will provide adequate space and facilities. The department has approved of a two-storey unit with a partial subgrade basement. A great deal of study has been given to the design of this building and I think it will be found to be economical. We envisage that there will be provision for the necessary safety measures in preparing antigens and sera to be used for the laboratory diagnosis of viral diseases, especially the neurotropic viruses, such as poliomyelitis and the viral encephalomy-elitides. I forgot to mention last night, when we were talking about the virus program, that sixty of the research projects provided for in Ontario in the past two years were carried out under the national health program. The virus section of the laboratory of hygiene will be in a position to assist the laboratory divisions of the provincial departments of health. We also anticipate that numerous research projects will include the development of improved diagnostic procedures for neurotropic virus diseases with particular emphasis on the poliomyelitis group of viruses.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister indicate the size of the building and the staff that will be employed there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I notice that in the report of the department to which I alluded earlier mention is made at pages 46 and 47 of the

many functions performed by the department under this particular vote. It is stated that technical aid is provided to a number of federal agencies, including crown companies, on occupational health matters. I gather that in times past there has been no attempt made to charge other government departments or crown companies for the services rendered to them by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am wondering if as a matter of true accounting to the public and to parliament it would not be better if that were done. We have many cases of this sort where work is done by one department for another department and a charge made accordingly. We are now told that crown companies are-going to pay income tax under the recent amendment to the Income Tax Act, and as an aid to clear accounting I am wondering: whether it would be desirable to make charges for this work.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Under item 269, which deals with the administration of the Food and Drugs Act, may I express the hope that by now the minister is in a position to make an informative and useful statement on a question that I have put to him quite a number of times.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Just a minute. My question relates-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Don't be hard on me. I am just trying to help my friend.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-to the matter of brown bread. As the minister knows from remarks I have made on this question before, I am not suggesting that any impurities are being put in bread but I do suggest that a form of deception develops owing to the fact that not all brown bread is whole wheat bread. It appears that some of it is white bread dyed brown. I do not mean to suggest that the materials with which it is dyed are impure or injurious to health, but certainly it is unfair that people should buy brown bread thinking that they are getting whole wheat bread when such is not the case. I have drawn this matter to the minister's attention a number of times. It was treated with some levity at first but gradually we have been getting fairly serious attention paid to it, and the -last two or three times the matter has been raised the reply has been that it would be discussed between the officials of the minister's department and the trade concerned.
It is good to know that progress is being made and that there are such discussions but I hope that the officials did not just listen to what the trade had to say but made some pretty definite suggestions to the trade as to what should be done in the interests of the people of Canada.
I have in my hand a copy of the report of the minister's department for the last year for which the report is available, the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951. I find in it a few interesting pages on the work of the inspection and enforcement services under the heading of food and drugs. The comments on pages 73 to 75 indicate that this division has been fairly active. For example, they have concerned themselves with the "molasses for health" fad. I note in the report this comment:
While vendors generally made no claims themselves, one, who did advertise that "if you suffer
Supply-Health and Welfare from heart troubles, high blood pressure or gallstones, try crude molasses," was prosecuted under section 6A of the Food and Drugs Act. Conviction was refused on the grounds that a recommendation to "try" a product was not a recommendation for treatment. The case was appealed and a conviction obtained.
There are two or three other interesting items such as this one:
A number of butchers and vendors in the Ottawa district were prosecuted for selling horsemeat; it is an offence to sell horsemeat without clearly labelling it as such, or to use it in the manufacture of sausages or to use it or any other meat, except beef, in hamburg steak. As it was apparent that the vendor had often acted in good faith, believing his product to be beef, section 24 of the act was invoked to bring charges against the wholesaler or supplier as third party.
There is another reference to a Cornwall cheese factory violating cheese holding regulations. It turned out there were weaknesses in the regulations and they are now under study. Then there is this reference:
As a result of a case where 2,800 gallons of maple syrup seized in Quebec were found to be adulterated with cane sugar, conferences were held with the federal and provincial departments of agriculture, and methods of close co-operation developed.
Then I read the following:
Special attention is being given to food colours, some of which in the past have represented a definite health hazard. This year a shipment of 150 pounds of food colour imported from England was found to be of a kind not permitted in foods and was returned to the exporter.
My reason for referring to these few examples listed in the report of the department is to suggest that what some of us are asking for is not out of line with the sort of thing that the department is already doing. I feel that while the matter of white bread dyed brown may not involve something that is actually injurious to health nevertheless it is most unfair that there is not some regulation requiring that a loaf of brown bread must be whole wheat bread and not white bread dyed brown. I hope that this time the minister has something definite and informative to tell us.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend hopes I will have something definite. He must not confuse his perfectly legitimate aspiration, with which I fully agree, with the practicalities of the situation. As the committee knows-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are we going to get elegant words again?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They are not only elegant but they are pregnant with true meaning.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Let the minister speak for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The minister may not be referred to in those terms any longer, although I will admit that for a long time I did believe that all brown bread was non-fattening, but
2982	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare I have learned through bitter experience that that is not the case. The committee knows that first reading has already been given in the other place to a bill to revise the Food and Drugs Act, and it is a rather important revision. It is not the intention to have the bill come into this house this year because we want a full discussion by outside interests of the implications of that measure.
My hon. friend has drawn my attention specifically to the question of bread. Incidentally, I think that the food and drugs division is perhaps one of the least known but one of the most important and most effective operations of the government of Canada. The committee will be interested in knowing that the Food and Drugs Act is one of our oldest statutes. In fact I think it was the second statute on our statute books. The public have no knowledge of this fact, and I am sure all members have not, but every type of food used in Canada is examined in some form or another by the sampling method through our system of continuous inspection. Canada has a reputation in the standard of its foods generally which I think is excelled by no country.
At the American food institute last September Canada was given first recognition among all countries in attendance at that conference not only for its administration but for the philosophy and purpose behind the Food and Drugs Act. With regard to the bread question, a meeting was called by the department on April 8 at which discussions were held with representatives of the consumers, bakers, millers and allied trades on proposed amendments to standards for flour and bread under the Food and Drugs Act. Following the discussions the proposed amendments are now being drafted. Actually the amendments that we had in our minds were not put forward in the form in which we were thinking about them but the principles were. We wanted to get the reaction because there is no point in hurting a trade simply for the purpose of passing a regulation. We try to administer this act on the basis of co-operation with the industry, and we find that brings good results both from their point of view and ours. So that we are now in the process, and drafting is pretty well complete. One of these days very soon I will submit to the governor in council the regulations we have in mind, and they will be tabled in this house. They are not ready at the moment but they will be complete.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I interrupt to get this clear? It seems to me that the minister is talking about two things: a bill to amend the act and proposed-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No, this has nothing to do with the bill. I just referred to the bill in order to pay tribute to the officers of the food and drugs division who have been working on it for a long time. I am now talking about the questions my hon. friend raised, and the questions I am dealing with have to do with this particular amendment. The amendment will deal with proposed standards for such items as wheat flour, whole wheat flour, brown bread, white bread and specialty bread.
As my hon. friend knows, there is some bread that does have less nutritional value than other bread. We are seeking to deal with that aspect of the situation. I believe I can say with assurance that labelling requirements for whole wheat bread in the new regulations will require a statement of the percentage of whole wheat flour used, and that this figure for percentage will be incorporated as part of the same. So, my hon. friend may feel assured that this matter is being faced up to.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that action is being taken and that new regulations are being drafted. The minister makes it clear, does he, that it will be definite that any whole wheat bread claiming to be whole wheat bread will have to be properly labelled? But would it still be possible, under the amended regulations, for brown bread to be put on the counters not labelled as whole wheat bread and not be whole wheat bread? It seems to me that is the problem.
We can understand that if you buy a wrapped loaf of bread and if the label says it is whole wheat bread, then you know.you are getting whole wheat bread; but how about the housewife who buys an unwrapped loaf of brown bread thinking she is getting whole wheat bread?

Before the minister does give his report, I want to make a few observations on this vote. I believe it is wise to be vigilant and try to prevent the importation, and of course the use, of illicit narcotics in this country. In recent years, as our relationship with the Pacific countries has been drawn more closely together, we are brought in touch with the origin of this terrible curse, because most of the opium is at present being grown and processed across the Pacific. Not many days ago I was speaking to a responsible officer who had returned from the Far East. He stated that narcotics were being distributed by the red army to their troops in order to build up their morale, and stimulate them to high endeavour when they made their mass attacks against the United Nations forces in Korea.
It was only a few years ago that the Japanese were greatly interested in the narcotics business. In their struggle to obtain control of China, they sought to corrupt the Chinese by the free distribution of heroin and other narcotics on the streets of Hong Kong and other ports. It was a studied policy of trying to undermine the morale of these people. The generalissimo of China is the only man of whom I know who had any effective way of curing addiction to these narcotics. He passed a law that the Chinese addicts who were found must be taken outside the city walls and have their heads cut off. Not many years ago there was an opium factory in Vancouver, and opium and these other narcotics were regarded as regular items of commerce between the nations.
We are indebted to the work of the late Prime Minister Mackenzie King, who proceeded to a conference in Shanghai in 1900, and to others, for an effort to control illicit traffic in narcotics throughout the world. As a result of the work done there, later followed up by the league of nations and now being further carried out by the United Nations, a strong effort is being made to control international trade in narcotics. We in British Columbia, with all our ports on the Pacific, are of course vulnerable to the

importation of these narcotics. An examination of our jail statistics, penitentiaries and schools for the correction of young men and women, will show that there is a very widespread addiction. I hope that the minister will give this matter greater attention, and that the vote may be increased.
In this connection I want to point out the good work that has been done by the attorney general of British Columbia, the Hon. Gordon S. Wismer, who has almost made it a life work to try to clean out peddlers and dealers in narcotics in the province of British Columbia. If we could suppress this thing we could take a great load off the taxpayers of this country. I want to say to the minister that some of these milder forms of sedatives, to my mind, are the thin edge of the wedge in popularizing the use of narcotics. I know that medical men prescribe these things, and in most cases there is a general addiction to headache wafers and to certain kinds of pills and other things which are readily available. I urge the minister to use every effort to get at the root of this thing, and purge Canada completely of the commerce of illicit narcotic dealers.

This is an important problem which has to be dealt with, not only by way of domestic but as well by way of international arrangements. We have been a member of the various narcotic conventions since their inception, both under the league of nations and now under the United Nations. Our officers have been recognized as very useful collaborators at that end. The problem of barbiturates is one that we are continually considering. My hon. friend knows, of course, the requirements as to prescriptions in that regard. However that phase of the matter is receiving our full attention. I fully agree with him as to what he said about the attorney general of British Columbia. That gentleman has evinced a very considerable interest in this whole problem, not only because of where he lives but because,
I would suppose, of his own professional experience as well. He has given my officers and me the greatest measure of co-operation, as indeed have all the attorneys general in our ten provinces.

I think it would be wrong to let the wrong impression go out from this chamber-and I am sure the hon. member for Eglinton did not intend that it should; there was some justification for what he said, because of press comment-but I should not like to. have the wrong impression go out. While the situation is serious, and will continue to be serious as long as people are using narcotic drugs illicitly, the situation is not one which would justify anyone saying that our teenagers, our young people, are using these drugs in improper quantities.
In fact, when these stories began to appear, I was concerned about the matter, and made inquiries in the two centres in the United States which may be regarded as the chief centres for the distribution of these illicit drugs. I am satisfied from my contacts there, and from what I know in this country, that those stories do not represent a situation that could be characterized in the generally exaggerated terms used. This does not mean to say that there are not cases-because there are. The use of codeine, of course, is not due entirely to illicit use, because codeine is found in medicines in common use. That explains in some measure the considerable use of this product.
One of the serious situations-and I hope what I say in this regard will get outside the chamber-is the development of some of the synthetic chemicals possessing potential addiction properties. They have no relation whatsoever to opium, the poppy or the coca plant. Those people who may be interested in this synthesis may be sure that the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in the United States, and the national revenue officers are aware of this situation. We may not know where all the centres are; but this matter is one that is being closely followed, and will be prosecuted with all the might that Canada and all other nations combined can bring to bear upon this unfortunate development. At the moment I shall not say more on this subject; but I do hope that what I have said will reach the proper sources.
The hon. member has directed my attention to the treatment of addicts in British Columbia. In the United States there are two centres, one located at Lexington and one at Fort Worth, where for ten or twelve years they have carried on treatment on an experimental basis. It was proposed that we should establish a similar centre in Canada. I was sympathetic with that point of view and that objective, because it is one thing to stop the use of these illicit drugs, one thing to find the person who sells them

Supply-Health and Welfare illicitly, and quite another to deal with curing those unfortunate individuals who become victims.
Provincial departments of health-and in this I include Mr. Wismer in British Columbia -have been interested in surveying this problem. I have sent two of my senior officers to visit both these institutions and to see the work done. Without deprecating what is being done there, I am afraid the evidence thus far does not support the claims-well, I shall not use the word "claims"-does not support the complete success of these ventures.
The cost is very considerable indeed and, on the basis of present evidence the results do not strike us as being fully satisfactory. However this is a problem -which must be faced, and we are studying it.

I notice that the vote for this item has gone up every year in the last five or six years, and I believe that as a result of that the health of Indians and the facilities for caring for them when they are ill have improved. I should like to compliment Dr. Moore, of the health of Indians branch, upon the work he has done in improving health services for our native population.
The increase this year in items 271 and 272 amounts to nearly $2 million, and that would seem to be a satisfactory situation. However, an examination of the details makes one wonder whether there has been or is likely to be a parallel increase this year in the health services provided for Indians. In looking over the details I notice there is an increase of only one medical officer. The number of graduate nurses is up from 236 last year to 261 this year. In my view that is


a commendable change. I am glad to see the health of Indians branch securing the services of more graduate nurses. That is one of the ways in which the health of Indians is likely to be improved.
While I am oni my feet I shall ask several questions, following which the minister can answer. The first of these questions is as to where the extra number of graduate nurses are to be employed. What is their use? Are they to be used in hospitals or at the nursing stations scattered about in various places?
Another of the details shows that ward aides and housemaids are to be supplied in greater number. I do not know the extent to which that would improve the health of Indians and I would ask the minister to comment on this point. How many of these ward aides and housemaids are Indians. One of the great weaknesses in the Indian affairs branch, it seems to me, is that an insufficient number of Indians are employed in this type of work when, in many cases, they could be employed satisfactorily. Thus far the number of Indians employed has been small indeed. That is one weakness which in the past has affected the Indian health service, and we should be making every improvement to get away from that condition.
Then I notice an item for firemen-labourers, which is increased from 22 to 45. How many of these are Indians? I find it difficult to understand why the number of firemen-labourers would have to be increased to more than double what it was. I also find it a little difficult to understand how this considerable increase in expenditure is going to improve the general health of the Indian population, or the way in which they are cared for.
Taking the whole list of details altogether, under the general heading that is given here for operation and maintenance, salaries and so on, you will find that the amount has gone from $2,531,000 odd to $3,217,000 odd or an increase of approximately $700,000. Then there is a note Which says that $193,000 is for increases in the rates of pay. In other words, the rest of it is for new people that were taken on since last year. I was somewhat disturbed to find that for these new people taken on there was an expenditure of over $500,000, or an increase in expenditure of over half a million dollars. In that amount there was only one more medical officer and there were some twenty odd more nurses. It seems to me that it is out of proportion when the expenditure of that $500,000 is not going to result in a parallel improvement in the health of the Indians or the facilities for taking care of them. It disturbs me more, if that is the case, which

is the conclusion that one would perhaps draw from this without any further explanation of it.
Another matter that I want to ask the minister about is the situation in regard to tuberculosis tests. We had some discussion on that last year. The minister gave us the figures of the number of people tested last year, the number tested to date and the incidence of tuberculosis in our Indian population. As is well known, the incidence of tuberculosis in the Indian population is very many times that of the rest of the population. It has been one of the greatest cripplers and killers so far as Indians are concerned, and is the greatest plague from the medical point of view which has to be fought by the particular branch whose estimates we are now considering. I would hope that the minister can produce figures which will show some improvement in the incidence of the tuberculosis rate from last year, and also that the program of chest X-ray of Indians has been completed. It certainly has been in process for some considerable time and should be completed by now.
In addition to the specific questions which I have asked at this point, perhaps it might be possible for the minister to make a general statement in regard to the affairs of this particular branch of his department; in other words, what has been accomplished by this branch throughout the year, and so forth. That might expedite proceedings by making it unnecessary for a number of questions to be asked which otherwise would have to be asked.

As my hon. friend has said, the great hospital program is one that is having tremendously satisfactory results in tuberculosis, as he knows from his knowledge of the problem. These are staffs that our officers deemed necessary to carry on the proper functioning of the hospitals. My hon. friend knows something of some of the hospitals in Alberta. As he knows, they are good hospitals, and there is no over-extravagance. They are not comparable in some respects with the material set-up of corresponding institutions, although the service is good and is one that this country can be proud of, in keeping with its duty, responsibilities, and one that we ought not to be afraid to boast about to nations of the world who complain that the western nations do not treat their native populations as they should.
The results of this whole program are seen, as my hon. friend mentioned, in the reduction of the tuberculosis rate. There is no doubt that tuberculosis among Indians is a very serious problem. And while we cannot always measure achievement by financial expenditure the fact is that since the government of Canada did take this increased interest in the problem of the native by building these new hospitals at very considerable expense, by the increase of staff-when you think that the budget now is some $13,500,000 for Indian help, and five years ago it was around $2,500,000, you cannot help seeing that there is a tremendous increase in the expenditure, and I think the results more than demonstrate what is being done.
We have not by any means successfully tackled this problem, but from coast to coast, through the private practitioner, the doctor, the nurses, those permanently and those parttime engaged in our services, by the results of the researches that are going on in tuberculosis, the co-operation with the provincial departments of health and so on, we are able

Supply-Health and Welfare to present I think a very satisfactory position. The death rate for tuberculosis has dropped 45 per cent in Indians, in five years. That is a tremendous achievement. It is not one for which I am taking credit or one for which I am seeking to give full credit to our officers. It is the result of combined effort on the part of many agencies. I could mention many. I am thinking now of the late Dr. Fred Tisdale of the Toronto Sick Children's Hospital, who devoted so much of his time and so much of his own resources to this problem. I mention this simply because he passed away two years ago and I neglected on that occasion to pay him the tribute that he deserved in connection with this program. He was associated with Dr. Vivian who, along with our own Dr. Moore, made that very important survey on Indian health that gave us the guide for much of the work that we have been able to do.
