This past year 75 per cent of the Indian population of 135,000 have received X-ray examinations.
Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is that the aggregate figure up to date? If so, there are 25 per cent of the Indians who have not yet been X-rayed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is this past year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What I am trying to get at is whether 75 per cent of the Indians were X-rayed last year or whether that is the aggregate figure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Last year roughly 75 per cent of the native population of the country received X-ray examinations. It is not stopping; it is unending.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I know that, but can the minister tell us what proportion of the Indian population has never had any X-ray examination?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Before we built the big hospital in the James bay area I can tell you, as the Vivian report pointed out, that the picture was one of which no one had reason to be very proud. I cannot give you the exact details of the numbers who have never been examined.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The reason I am asking these questions is because I am afraid that what happens is that the same people were X-rayed this year as were X-rayed last year. That is quite all right and is necessary in a large number of cases. I am not complaining about that, but what happens is that people who have never been X-rayed continue without being X-rayed. The result is that a large section, probably some 20 per cent on the basis of the figures the minister has given, has never been X-rayed and tuberculosis still runs wild amongst them to a large extent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are extending our services as fast as we can.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What I should like to know from the minister is what steps are being taken to cover the	20	per cent	who so far,shall we say, have	escaped	his	toils in this
regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
We are seeking to extend our services just as quickly as we can get personnel and the money to do these things. I agree 1,000 per cent with everything my hon. friend has said. I read an editorial the other day in which someone was referring to the money we were spending on Indian health. I am going	to	send	that editorial tomy hon. friend, and I	hope	he	will be good
enough to join with me in writing to the editor and explaining why we are spending it. We can extend these services only if we have more personnel and equipment, but that costs money. The government has to take into consideration its over-all obligations. I regard
2990	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare this as one of the most important. I thank my hon. friend for giving the support to this measure that he has, and I know that if the budget is increased next year he will agree with me that it is a perfectly legitimate expenditure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As the minister has indicated, not only have I never criticized any increase but in most years I have asked for a greater increase because I am aware of the crying need for the expansion of Indian health services. I have another question of a different nature. The amount appropriated last year, as shown at page 41 of the estimates, was $9,875,000 for operation and maintenance and $1,609,000 for construction or acquisition of buildings. In the table the minister put on Hansard last night the figure for expenditures for operation and maintenance is $10,735,000 which is just about $1 million more than we voted. The figure for construction or acquisition of buildings is $924,000 which is $700,000 less than we voted last year. Can he explain how he got the extra money in the one case and what happened to the remainder of the vote in the other case?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In the first case we got almost a million dollars in the further supplement-aries last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They are not included here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No. As to the $700,000 in the other case, the answer is that it is due to construction delays.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As an Indian chief I congratulate the minister for the statement he has made that 75 per cent of the Indian population have been X-rayed. Is that true?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Ugh!

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As an Indian chief I thank you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are in the same boat. I doubt whether 75 per cent of the paleface population of Canada have been X-rayed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are you an Indian chief?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If you are not an Indian chief then don't enter this debate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are two main reservations in Nova Scotia, one at Eskasoni and the other at Shubenacadie. I should like to ascertain from the minister how the department is doing in gathering all the Indians into those two reservations. The reason I ask the question is that there was a reservation at Why-cocomagh and the Indians there were inclined to go to Eskasoni.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend will appreciate that is a matter for the Indian affairs branch. That does not come under me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You handle the maintenance of these Indians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Just health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In connection with the exchange which has just taken place between two Indian chiefs, as just an ordinary Indian I should like to make a remark. It is simply "ugh".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That has long since been remarked.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Looking at the details on page 336 I see that the estimate last year for travelling expenses was $115,000 and it is the same for this year. How much of the $115,000 last year was actually expended?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The amount expended was $169,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Then if $169,000 was
required last year why do you keep using the same figure of $115,000? Do you expect there will be considerably less travelling this year than last?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are hoping to cut our travel costs, but I am afraid we are going to have to ask for supplementaries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to comment that I think the figure that is put in the estimates for our consideration should be one that bears a fairly close relationship to the experience of the department under this particular item in the previous year. A general figure should not be put in the estimates which is the same this year as last year, but rather a figure which the department thinks represents the amount they will actually expend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is pretty difficult to foresee an epidemic, you know.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I would complain somewhat about that method of preparing the estimates. Underneath that there is an item for educational and informational publications. Last year the amount was $3,500 and this year it is $5,000. Would the minister tell us what those publications are and for whom they are designed? Are they for the education of the Indians, or to educate the white people about the Indians?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
My hon. friend was here last night when the hon. member for Eglinton was engaged in criticizing one of these publications. I will ask my hon. friend who has iust spoken for whom he thinks they were designed, if he was criticizing the low I.Q.

quality of them. Obviously they are directed to try to reach the population concerned. The item involves film strips, posters and displays, one poster on a proper breakfast, one poster on a proper lunch, one poster on a proper supper and two placards done in a form and employing techniques that it was thought would reach the population concerned. The same is true of the film strips.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You are now talking about the next subitem, educational and informational material other than publications, $10,000, are you not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I thought you were talking about that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, the $5,000 item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is an instructional handbook on practical hygiene that we have put out for the Indians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It just covers one publication?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would tell us something about what happened to the four Indian girls who were sent to Australia to take a midwifery course. That was an experiment, and I would like to know whether it worked out well or whether it was a failure. I think it was about three years ago that they were sent to either Australia or New Zealand.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There were four of them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: One of them is now in our employ at our hospital at Fort Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan. I am sorry I cannot say what has happened to one of them but two did not come back.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Was it New Zealand they went to?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister comment on the position of the Eskimos now? A report came out in the newspapers expressing some concern about the health of those people. We do know that the Eskimo is a declining race but I wonder if the minister would say a word as to their health?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The Eskimo is not now a disappearing race of human beings. Their population is increasing at the rate of about 1J per cent per year now. Undoubtedly that is due to improved medical attention, although we are not reaching them as effectively as we might because of the location of the population. There are about seven or eight thousand Eskimos, and with the moneys and facilities at our disposal, we are greatly interested in their welfare, as we are interested in the welfare of the Indians.
Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There is just one other subitem about which I would like to ask. I see that laundry and other sundry items is down from $130,000 to $100,000. That laundry bill, I presume, is for washing sheets and so on in the hospitals. I was just going to ask the minister in what way it was cut down. The answer might prove an example to other departments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember the discussion in the house last year and how one hon. member criticized the request for moneys to purchase some laundry machines. There was one we were putting in at a cost of about $60,000. We installed one at Nanaimo with another one at Coqualeetza, and another one at Fort Qu'Appelle. We have cut down the bill because we are doing our own laundry with good machines.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Indians and Eskimos health services-
272.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,814,400.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister tell us what the construction or acquisition program was last year? In other words what buildings were actually acquired or built, and what is the program for this year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I gave the program for this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not remember that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I did when I answered you earlier. I mentioned Norway House, Sardis, and the power house at Coqualeetza. I gave you that. Construction last year was: an enlarged health centre at Hazelton, British Columbia; a laundry building at Nanaimo, British Columbia; major repairs at Miller Bay, British Columbia; completion of the hospital at Hobbema, Alberta; extensive progress on the addition to the hospital at Fort Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan; extensive progress in the construction of a hospital at Norway House, rehabilitation, Fisher river Indian hospital; completion of health centres at the following places: Lansdowne House; Pikangi-kum, Ontario; Christian Island, Ontario; Ruperts House; Seven Islands, Quebec; and Shubenacadie.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
273.	Special technical services, $401,710.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There has been a change in the form of the estimates in respect of this item from last year. Last year "special technical services" was the heading of a group of estimates and then we had the following items under that in the main part of the book of estimates: nutrition, child and maternal
2992

Supply-Health and Welfare health, venereal disease control, dental health, hospital design and consulting service, mental health, blindness control, and civil aviation medicine.
Only one of those items listed in the main estimates last year still remains in the main estimates this year. We have already passed that item-item 268, epidemiology, including the former venereal disease control. When one looks for those other items that were listed in the main estimates last year he finds them now merely as details in the back of the book; in this instance they are to be found on page 337. I would be glad to have the minister's comment as to why this change was made. It seems to me it was better to have those individual sections of the work of this branch listed in the main items themselves.
While I am on my feet I should like to say a bit about one of the special technical services. They are broken down into details in two ways. First of all they are broken down in regard to the various types, and then they are broken down again in these various headings: nutrition, child and maternal health, etc. My question relates to one of the sections, namely nutrition. As I indicated to the minister when we were back on another item, there has been a reduction in the amount allotted for nutrition from $144,069 to $122,358 this year.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, this is a field in which very useful and worth-while research could be pursued. I think we are realizing more and more that preventive measures in the field of health do improve with studies in proper nutrition. I have read with interest the section of the last annual report, under the heading of nutrition, found on pages 44 to 46. While I find it interesting, it seems to me from reading that section that with a little more money and a little more encouragement still more might be done by the nutrition division of the department. Here is a paragraph on page 45 that I will call to the minister's attention:
The table of food values recommended for use in Canada was first issued in 1946 because no compilation of Canadian information on this subject existed. Even now only some of the figures are strictly Canadian. A special design for this booklet was developed and much new information was obtained on weights and measures of foodstuffs. A complete revision was carried out during the year and calorie values were recalculated in terms of the new factors recommended by the food and agriculture organization.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is a field in which more research might be done and in which valuable information might be made available to our people. Surely nutrition is basic to our health. In connection with the comment the minister made a little while ago,

I may point out that health should not be judged by girth-mine as against his-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mine is like yours.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We have come a lot closer together in the last couple of years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is that good?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Whether it is good or not depends on how that relationship is defined. At any rate, he is much thinner, and I have not gone the other way. Further in this same section on nutrition I note this:
Only one nutrition survey was carried on during the year, the study of a typical county in southwestern Ontario, carried out in the Elgin-St. Thomas health unit. Such surveys, the most extensive work of this type now being done in Canada, are carried on as a co-operative effort by the federal, provincial and local governments and serve to stimulate interest in nutrition and health generally. At the same time, by screening a group for nutritional defects, they assist in estimating the extent of malnutrition existing in Canada. If carried out in areas selected as being typical of the country as a whole, as recommended by the Canadian council on nutrition, such surveys would provide a comprehensive over-all picture of nutritional conditions in Canada.
The wording of that paragraph implies that more could be done, and if more were done it would be useful. The inference is that when those who wrote this report endeavoured to put down what work is being done under the heading "nutrition" they had to admit that it left room for much more work to be done. That being the case, I do not like to see the amount being reduced. I want to emphasize the fact that, as I see it, our interest in nutrition should not be only in obvious cases of malnutrition, but our interest should be in finding out what are the best types of foods for us to be eating for the development of the health of our people. I would be glad to hear from the minister on these various points.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The consolidation of these votes took place because it is part of our general policy to absorb the funds of these divisions into one main vote. We have been able to save about $14,000 as a result of that effort. I would -hope to hear a lot of tributes paid to that effort, because it has not in any way interfered with the objectives which we had in mind.
I can tell the hon. member that if there was a reduction in the federal item, it does not in any way represent a lessening of activity. We feel we have on hand sufficient stocks of certain informational material to cover our operations for this year, and that is largely the reason for the reduction. We had more than one survey under way this year. There was the one to which my hon. friend referred, and there has been a nutritional survey going

on in Manitoba dealing with dental conditions and so on. Last year was the fourth of a five-year study at six Indian schools, and there was also a survey dealing with nutritional therapy for blindness. In 1952-53 we have in mind three more nutritional surveys, one among Quebec school children. Then we have a project for a mental and dental examination at six Indian residential schools, which will complete the five-year study. Then there will be a continuing study of blindness, including nutritional therapy. The hon. member may be sure there is no lessening of the work of this division.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is the same answer the minister gave me the last time I complained about a reduction in the amount for this division. I hope that is the case, but as I say my reading of the latest report available suggests that there is room for more activity there. In the light of the paragraph of the report which says that even now only some of the figures in the table of recommended food values are strictly Canadian, may I ask the minister whether there has yet been prepared a strictly Canadian table of recommended food values?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the minister not think it might be a good idea to pursue that project?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that no one on the continent has a better reputation as a nutritional expert than Dr. Pett. He has made no submission to me that I have turned down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: But the minister has turned down some of my submissions.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
274.	Health insurance studies and administration of general health grants, $74,305.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This is the item, Mr. Chairman, upon which the minister last night suggested we continue our very interesting discussion on health plans.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That was my understanding.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What I said was that I would be glad to give my hon. friend a further explanation of my statement that his proposal did not appear to me to be satisfactory. That is quite different from the general debate on the item, upon which we have already had a general discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Then I shall deal with a couple of matters we discussed in regard to my proposal, which I understand the minister is quite agreeable to discussing now. In describing the plan that has been in operation 55704-1894
Supply-Health and Welfare in Sweden for the past 25 years when I was speaking last night I said the following, as found on page 2952 of Hansard for June 5:
It calls for the patient to pay 25 per cent of the doctor, dentist or hospital bill, with the remaining 75 per cent to be paid out of a health insurance fund maintained by regular contributions by all those who are financially able to contribute. The 25 per cent which is paid by the patient-
Then the minister interrupted and said:
It is the other way around.
As I understand that, Mr. Chairman, the minister implies that under the Swedish health insurance plan the patient pays 75 per cent of the cost of the doctor, dentist, or hospital bill, and the health insurance fund pays 25 per cent; is that correct?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Now, that is very interesting-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I misunderstood the question. What was the question again?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In outlining the plan, I said the following:
It calls for the patient to pay 25 per cent of the doctor, dentist or hospital bill, with the remaining 75 per cent to be paid out of a health insurance fund maintained by regular contributions by all those who are financially able to contribute. The 25 per cent which is paid by the patient-
Then the minister interrupted and said:
It is the other way around.
The question I just asked the minister was, is it correct that he claims that under the Swedish plan the patient pays 75 per cent?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, no; the patient pays everything, and then he gets a two-thirds refund.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister said it was just the other way around, implying that the patient pays 75 per cent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What else does that mean, if it is the other way around.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You take it as you want it, but I am telling you what the facts are. I am trying to help my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am trying to straighten the minister out. He interrupted a quite sensible plan that I was putting forward-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not agree that it is a sensible plan. I do not want to adopt it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I did not say the minister did want to adopt it. I am putting it forward as what I think is a sensible plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does it represent the point of view of your party?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It represents my point of view, I said over and over that it is my idea of a sensible plan. It is the only plan that has

Supply-Health and Welfare been put forward by anybody in this house, so far as I know, because the minister has never stated what he thinks is a good plan or a bad plan for health insurance. All we have ever heard for the last 33 years is when we are told just before an election that we will be given health insurance; that is all we have heard. I believe it is time we heard from the minister, after the tremendous amount of money and time that have been put into study by his department during the last six years, as to what he believes is a good health plan.
The point I should like to straighten out with the minister is this. When I was describing this health plan, that has been in successful operation in Sweden for 25 years, the minister interrupted me and said, as reported at page 2952 of Hansard:
My hon. friend has referred to the Swedish scheme, and in order to know exactly what his position is I should like to know whether he is in favour of the new act in Sweden . . .
I take it he was implying there is a new act that is in the process of going into operation, and the old one is being discarded.
I refer again to page 8 of the minister's own publication, "Health insurance in Sweden", social security series memorandum No. 10, produced by the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. At page 8, in referring to this new plan under the heading "Proposed program" it says:
Legislation was passed in 1946, which would bring about a universal .compulsory program, mainly state-supported. The reform has not been brought into force, and is now postponed indefinitely.
That was six years ago. They have not put it in for six years. I think it was passed then, and it has now been postponed indefinitely. Yet the minister has tried to leave the impression that it was just on the verge of going in, and he backed that up by saying, when I asked him to comment on the Swedish plan, "I do not think very much of it, nor do many people in Sweden".
What I say is that the people in Sweden have had the present plan in operation for 25 years and they have not changed it, though they could have done so. So far as I can see there is no possibility of their changing it. So I say there are a lot of people in Sweden who do like it. I say the people in Sweden consider that this is a very satisfactory plan.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You say; but that is not the fact.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: All you have to do is to ask the people who live there-the doctors, the dentists, the people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Have you done that?
tMr. Hees.]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, I have.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Well, I have right in front of me now perhaps the greatest authority on health insurance on this continent, and my statement was based upon a memorandum which he gave me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Well, all I can say is that it is very strange that the Swedish people have kept this plan for 25 years, and that they seem to be in process of keeping it for a great many more years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And you are in favour of it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
If it were so bad, why have they not thrown it out and put in this much more desirable plan, according to the minister? I want to know that.
Now let us get on to the health studies covered by this vote. As I understand the vote, it is to provide money so the minister and his officials can examine all matters pertaining to health insurance, can study plans from other countries that have been in operation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is one of the reasons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is to help his officials decide which would be the best plan for this country, in their opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is one of their many functions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And a very important one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Undoubtedly; but they also administer the national health grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister has held his portfolio for six years. So far as I can find out these studies have been going on for about that length of time. Yet so far to my knowledge we have not heard any of the results of the studies these votes have paid for. A report from the minister to the people of this country is long overdue.

I notice this company is being granted the right to carry on many types of insurance activity. Personally I think we have plenty of insurance companies in Canada today in the field in which this company is seeking a charter.
Take automobile insurance, for example. I think anyone who drives a car in any province in Canada, with the possible exception of the province of Saskatchewan, will agree that some governmental action, either provincial or federal, is necessary in that field, particularly when you realize how car insurance costs have risen during the last ten years. The great majority of people in the low income groups find it almost impossible to insure a car today, and my opinion is that it is pretty nearly time the federal government should do something about it, as the provinces do not appear to be doing very much. Perhaps the provinces cannot do very much about it when these national charters are granted giving companies the right to operate from province to province right across the dominion.
If you take a look at the casualty list on the highways over the week ends I know you will say there is either something wrong with the drivers or with a lot of the cars which are on the highways. However, I think some yardstick or measure of automobile insurance is necessary in this country because the average policy one has to take from the old line companies for a passenger car, covering collision, public liability, and so forth, will run from $135 to $150. The average person may be able to secure his licence, and pay the instalments on his ear, but when it oomes to putting that car on the road and paying the rates demanded by insurance companies today he finds that almost impossible. In most provinces in this country that type of insurance is compulsory. Although they will sell you a licence and you may put your car on the road, you can drive that car only until you

have an accident. Then, under most provincial laws covering the matter, the R.C.M.P. have the right to pull you up and if you have not public liability insurance on the car, for which you must pay $130 to $150 your car may be confiscated, impounded and sold to pay the damage.
While the average person on the highway may be as careful as he likes, if someone who is not covered smashes into him then his car is in the garage with adjusters running around for months arguing about who is responsible and who is not responsible. Regardless of the fact that you may be insured by one of these companies, nine times out of ten if you are involved in an accident you have to hire a lawyer and go to court to prove that you have a right to your insurance.
If we are going to continue to grant charters on a national scale-and here I am thinking of automobile insurance particularly because it sticks out like a sore thumb- some governmental action must be taken. That insurance is compulsory in the provinces, but nothing is done, until you tear into somebody. Then the R.C.M.P. come into the picture, court action is necessary, and there is litigation all over the place. I think it is pretty nearly time the federal government at least set up some machinery to make an appraisal of automobile insurance in this country, particularly in view of the fact that the provinces are not doing it, to determine whether automobile insurance is being sold on a fair and reasonable basis that does not mean just a lot of money to the companies selling insurance and very little protection to the average person who is buying that insurance.
I am not quarrelling about the rest of the insurance here but I am particularly interested and concerned about automobile insurance because it is running way beyond the reach of the average person. I think the time has come when the provincial governments should set up their own insurance offices and, when a person takes out a licence for his car, if they are going to make insurance compulsory when the licence is granted it should be accompanied by an insurance policy which is fair, reasonable, and within the financial limits of the average person who is taking a car out on the highway. Anyone who cannot afford a policy should not take a car out on the road.

maintopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this bill has been before the house now for some time. This committee is dealing with Bill No. 62, an act to incorporate the Boundary Pipeline Corporation. At this time we are dealing with section 1. I should like to know from the chairman whether he is going to allow a general debate on the first section, or on each section as we go along. We have had different rulings on that, and probably we shall get a new one on this pipe-line bill.

maintopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: I do not know whether or not the names of those who are applying for the incorporation have been placed on the record, but I find that their names are as follows: George Herbert Barr, solicitor; William Purdon Cumming, solicitor; Robert Milliken Barr, solicitor; Archibald Turner Brown, managing director, and what else I do not know, and Frank Benjamin Poutney, investment dealer, all from that great city of Regina in Saskatchewan. These are to be the directors. In other words, these five men come to parliament and ask that they be made into one body, and that body to be called the Boundary Pipeline Corporation; or, putting it in shorter terms, they are to be called the company. In the incorporation clause they also say that there are a great many other persons who may become shareholders. All these other persons are unknown to your committee, Mr. Chairman. These five gentlemen alone are seeking the incorporation, and are to be called the company.

maintopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

maintopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
You will have a chance after awhile. Quite a number of speeches have
Boundary Pipeline Corporation been made with reference to this incorporation. In checking them over I have found that very few have endorsed these directors, but I am not taking objection to them. Like those who have spoken before me in reference to this bill, I take objection to the principle of it, and I shall endeavour to tell the committee my reasons for so doing.
I said a moment ago that there did not seem to be very many champions of this bill on the government side of the house. I might add here that those who are against it have given very good reasons, in my opinion, why the bill should not pass. When the bill passes, if it ever does, it will be a question of time before we know whether they have been given the proper authority or not.
We all know that this deals with something that is very important to Canada. It deals with the national products of Canada, the natural resources. In the past two or three years, and probably a little longer, attention has been turned as never before to the great natural resources of this country. For instance, the eyes of the world are fixed on the great discoveries and the great development of the natural products of some of the western provinces, particularly on Alberta and Saskatchewan with their oil and gas. Because of that, we find speculators of all kinds coming in; and, as I think we have in this case, speculators are seeking to incorporate a company to move gas from Saskatchewan to some other place. They are quite prepared to build their pipe line into Manitoba and on in to the city of Winnipeg. When they get there by way of an all-Canada route they immediately want to turn south and take their supply of gas down into the United States.
I would have no objection to a pipe-line company asking for a charter of that kind if there was sufficient gas in the west to supply Canada first. In this case it becomes a question of Canada first. We would be very wise in this country if we went to our neighbours to the south and extracted a leaf from their book of success and learned of the development of their country and their natural resources. If we were to take a leaf out of their book I am sure we would look to our own interests, and it would be Canada first.
I congratulate the great country to the south for having such a policy and carrying it into effect. After they have supplied their own people they are always willing to sell their surplus. However, their plan has been to develop the United States first. Let us copy that idea and let us make our slogan Canada first.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was directing the attention of the minister to the fact that some very valuable studies of health insurance have been carried on by virtue of the money we vote under this item. In particular I pointed out that the annual departmental report states that special attention has been given to the health insurance plans in Great Britain, New Zealand, Sweden and Denmark. I feel that the committee has the right to expect a statement from the minister at this time as to his views on the plans in effect in those countries and what he feels would be the best type of health insurance plan for Canada in the light of this study. He should also tell us when the point will be reached at which the studies for which we have been spending this money across the years will be converted into action, namely a health insurance program for this country.
Furthermore, I would point out that under this item of health insurance studies, health and sickness surveys have been conducted in the various provinces. Last evening I drew to the attention of the minister a recommendation made in the Saskatchewan health survey report which was prepared as part of the work of the health insurance studies division. Notably I drew attention to the fact that that report recommended a nationwide program of health insurance and in particular it recommended that if all the provinces were not ready to participate in such a plan, nevertheless a national plan should be established so the provinces ready to participate might do so. A reference is made to these health survey reports on page 62 of the minister's departmental report, which reads:
Exceedingly valuable material will be made available through the health and sickness surveys now being carried on by the provinces, which will give very much more complete data than any hitherto available on existing health services, and prevalence of illness and disability.
We have the departmental report saying that special attention is being paid to New Zealand, Great Britain, Sweden and Denmark, and the minister in that report saying that it has been valuable to get the information


contained in the health survey reports from the provinces, in one of which is the recommendation that there be a nation-wide program of health insurance.
I think the minister will agree that we are entitled to a statement as to his opinion, not only of the studies made in these other countries but of the recommendation made in the Saskatchewan health survey report. Not only should he give us the benefit of his views on the basis of this study; he should tell us how soon we can expect the enactment of a nation-wide program of health insurance.
