speechtext: I promised the hon. gentleman that I would tell him briefly what in my judgment was wrong with the plan he put forward-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister is now referring to the hon. member for Broadview.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: -with regard to Sweden, and I shall also state what I think is wrong with the plan put forward by the hon. member who has just spoken.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I understood the minister was going to outline his ideas on the British plan and also give us his ideas on a plan for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall have to decide what I am to say. My hon. friend is exercising his right as a member of the opposition and 1 am exercising what I conceive to be my duty in the light of government policy and other circumstances, and as a minister of the government. The plan my hon. friend put forward is limited to persons in good health between the ages of 14 and 40. It does not deal with the age group from birth to 14 in the non-dependent class, a most significant age group in our population. It does not provide for medical or hospital care for the age group over 40, and particularly the group from 60 to 70 and 80 years of age, which is another equally important group in the population of any country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I correct the minister on that. On page 5 of his memorandum, talking about the present program he says:
At the present time, everyone between the ages of 14 to 40 years of age, and in "good health," is eligible for membership In a local sickness fund. Married women must insure themselves independently of their husbands, and the couple may insure their children under 15 years.
Actually a parent has to insure a child; the child does not insure himself.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Under that plan only the age group 14 to 40 years is covered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Children are insured by their parents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I beg to differ with my hon. friend. The plan just covers that group. Anyone who has given thorough consideration to this matter will realize how inadequate that would foe. That particular program is not a health insurance program at all; it is a cash sickness maintenance scheme which may require a waiting period of 90 days on admission to membership before eligibility for benefits is obtained. The great weakness in that plan is that it covers about 50 per cent, or at best 60 per cent of the population.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Sixty per cent, so the memorandum says.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Sixty per cent of the population generally, and there have been years when it covered as low as 32 per cent of the population. In view of those limitations I cannot take any other stand than the one I took last night, that this proposal is not a health insurance scheme at all; it is simply a scheme of providing for a method of financing whereby the individual pays the full fee and receives two-thirds as reimbursement from the government or the state. I am sure that plan is not one that would commend itself to any group in this country that has given the matter serious consideration.
The question before us is of the greatest importance and has many implications. Our situation in this country is different from that in Sweden, New Zealand or the United Kingdom. Under our constitution the provinces are endowed with the primary responsibility for matters of health. I am sure no one would suggest that we embark upon a scheme of health insurance in Canada without the co-operation of a substantial portion of the provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That goes without saying.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend says that goes without saying, but he did not mention it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are some things so obvious that you do not have to mention them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will just
allow me to finish my argument, he may say all he feels like saying after he hears what I have said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The minister interrupted me
freely all afternoon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This matter is something that has to be considered in the light of our constitution. At no time has this government taken any other position, nor has the party of which my hon. friend is so distinguished a member. Just think what would happen if the central government of Canada, without regard for the provinces, embarked upon a scheme which in part touched a phase of
Supply-Health and Welfare their exclusive constitutional competence. Under the constitution of this country hospitals and eleemosynary institutions are the declared reserve of the provinces. You cannot have a hospital insurance scheme nor can you have an adequate medical insurance scheme unless the hospitals of the country are part and parcel of the plan. There is no question where the party of which I am a member stands. We have advocated health insurance in our platforms as an objective. That was done, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, in the platform of 1919. It was mentioned in the platform of the convention at which the present Prime Minister was made the leader of this party. But that does not mean to say that because a party has a plank in its platform, it has got to be done overnight.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Well, do it within ten years, or fifteen years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No hon. member will find any word of mine at any time where I said that this matter would be brought in without the proper foundation being laid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is the trouble.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I have had now for six years the responsibility of administering this department, and my relations with all the provinces have been most satisfactory. I think I may say I have an adequate understanding of the difficulties involved. Those difficulties are not the attitudes of the provinces, but there is also the matter of the necessary facilities to make this program work. I picked up the Ottawa Journal tonight, as I am sure other members did, and saw on the third page a headline pointing out the serious shortage of hospital beds in the Ottawa civic hospital. That situation is true not only of that great hospital but of most hospitals particularly in the larger centres of the country.
The reason the more meritorious scheme in Sweden has not been implemented, although it is the law, is because of the shortage of hospital beds and hospital personnel, particularly doctors. If you want to damn a scheme at the beginning all you have to do is give it immediate effect without having taken the necessary preparatory steps. When the former prime minister announced this program in May of 1948 he referred to the need of doing something in this important field. His whole life was one that demonstrated his soundness of judgment and faith in his declarations in the matter of health.
It is interesting to note what has happened since the introduction of that plan. At that time we estimated that we were short some 65,000 hospital beds in Canada. We embarked
3008	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare on a program of assistance to the provinces in the construction of hospitals. Since that time we have been able to assist the provinces in the provision of over 38,000 hospital beds. That is a tremendous achievement. When that objective was stated it was argued in this house that it could not possibly be reached in a five year period. Not only have we assisted in the provision of that number of beds, but 433 new hospitals of varying sizes have been built in this country in the past four years.
In addition, when we announced this plan we sat down with the ten provincial governments, surveyed the whole scene as best we could and set for ourselves certain objectives. One of the great shortages at that time was in personnel, both in the provincial departments and in the various health groups. Our national health program has resulted in the provision of 4,500 additional provincial government health officials in this country, research people, hospital administrators, nurses, psychologists, occupational therapists and the like. These 4,500 are paid entirely out of the moneys voted for this program.
In addition we have provided over 3,500 additional health workers, individuals who are attached to local health units, individuals who are engaged in work respecting arthritis, tuberculosis control and cancer control, all supplementing the health personnel of the provincial governments. Under this program rural health care is being brought closer to the level of that in urban areas, so much so that the deputy minister of health of the province of Ontario referred to this program at a recent meeting as one that had brought rural health care to a higher level than at any time in the history of his province.
Most of these new projects were and are paid for out of the national health program. The committee will understand that the program provides for outright grants except in the case of cancer control and hospital construction, where the principle of matching with the provinces is entertained and serves as a condition precedent. I think I can say that the program has resulted in putting new life into provincial campaigns to lessen child and maternal mortality, to control diseases like diphtheria and typhoid, and to counter the great cripplers, polio, arthritis and rheumatism. As the hon. member for Lanark said last night in his excellent speech, we have to face the fact that the infant mortality rate in this country, while it has improved in the last decade, is still behind that of Iceland and some other countries. That problem has to be met and is being met under this program as I have indicated.

The provincial governments are now enabled as a result of the financial assistance we give them to add new divisions to extend the scope of their public health services. For instance, right here close to Ottawa, in the county of Carleton, the county health unit is paid for half by the federal government and half by the county. There are many health units in the province of Ontario. Until the advent of this program most of the health units were paid for by the province and by the county concerned. This project provides assistance for extensions of existing programs or for new programs. The local unit in Carleton county was an extension of a program. We pay half the cost and the county the other half, thereby relieving the province of its financial responsibility for that particular area.
Likewise the provincial laboratory in the city of Ottawa is now being replenished with new and needed equipment under this program. Then there is the amount of equipment provided in our mental institutions and the number of occupational therapists who have been trained. In the Whitby mental hospital alone, one of the very good mental institutions of this country, you will find that we have provided equipment costing almost $300,000 to give the directors there an opportunity to provide more up-to-date care for the mentally ill. We are engaged in a program of building mental health clinics throughout the country. As the hon. member for Lanark and the hon. member for Eglinton said, mental illness is one of the great challenges that face many countries of the western world. The largest single grant in the national health program is for mental health.
When one realizes that 50 per cent of the bed occupancy in this country is by people suffering from mental illness, one gets an appreciation of the immensity of the problem. We have assisted in the provision of 8,000 mental hospital beds under this program. We have already provided under the mental health program fourteen mental health clinics, the idea being to try to reduce the number of people who go into these institutions. We want to see if we cannot cut down the population in the mental institutions. Our aim is to have a program of prevention to deal with people before they have to go to such institutions, or prevent them from going altogether. Experience of countries which have carried on this program has revealed that mental health clinics attached to hospitals or to public health units are capable of dealing with and anticipating many cases, in both adults and children, in this advanced way. That program is one we are very anxious to see in full operation. All these

things are a very important part of any medical or hospital care insurance program.
When we began this program we did not wait until the surveys were undertaken. The government had given consideration to that. At first we took the view that we should not inaugurate the plan until we had a careful assessment of the problem as it was seen in the provinces, but we knew there were certain things which had to be done. And we knew there were conditions precedent to ultimate action. We went ahead and built hospital beds, provided additional medical research, did something about crippling conditions among children, assisted the provincial governments and the voluntary organizations in their tuberculosis programs, did something about mental health, and did something about general public health. We went ahead on the basis of the facts as we knew them but, at the same time, we said to each provincial government: We would like you to undertake a survey in your province to see what the situation is, as it is seen not only by your officials but as well by the most qualified people in the field. As they come in I am tabling in this house the various health survey reports which have taken some three and a half years to prepare. The federal government provided $500,000 to the provinces for that purpose.
I am sure very few hon. members have had the opportunity of reading any of those reports completely because they are monumental documents, but those who have looked at them will realize the great effort and study that has been put into them. We find now that we underestimated the number of hospitals needed in many parts of this country. All one has to do is to look at the Ontario health survey report and one will see that we underestimated the number of beds which it is thought in this report will be required.
The recommendations in all these reports are very germane to this discussion now. My hon. friend, the member for Broadview, agreed that we could not do anything in this field without consulting the provinces, and that it would be unwise to embark immediately on a program without having provincial action. But the province of Ontario has made no recommendation about health insurance at the present time. As the member for Winnipeg North Centre said, only two survey reports thus far have urged the kind of scheme that has been discussed here today, the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta.
If my hon. friend wanted to pursue the plan he has been so assiduously promoting, he would have some considerable influence with
Supply-Health and Welfare the premier of the first province of the country, the largest province. I am sure that to the minister of health of the province of Ontario his views would be of great interest. The gentlemen in the provinces have to look at the problem in the same light we do. It is a problem that has an objective which we want to achieve, but it can be achieved only when preparatory steps have been taken, so that when the objective is achieved the scheme does not fall down simply because preparatory steps have not been taken.
These surveys are of the greatest importance but no one has emphasized that except the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He has only referred to the recommendations of two provinces, but that is because I am sure he has not had a chance to give careful analysis to the other recommendations, or even to read the other reports. When the house sees the report of the province of Quebec and that of the province of Nova Scotia they will realize that it is one thing to get up and say we must do something, and another to realize you have the responsibility for proposed action. You may want to see a thing done but you also want to see it work well. You do not rush into a scheme of the immense proportions we have here without laying the foundation. My hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue asked what I thought was a very appropriate question last night. He asked the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre: How are you going to finance the scheme? That is a very important consideration.
My views on this matter are well known. I have spoken of them in this house and elsewhere long before I came to this house. My views on the subject are known all over this country. I certainly would not want to embark upon a scheme until that scheme was ready to be embarked upon. I certainly would not want to embark upon it unless I knew we could count on the co-operation- not only co-operation by word of mouth but co-operation in dollars and cents-of the provinces themselves, and of the people of this country.
A scheme such as my hon. friend has been talking about and such as has been discussed generally here is one that will envisage contributions from three sources: from the federal government, from the provincial governments, and from individuals. When the Prime Minister announced this program four years ago, what was the situation in the world? We did not have a defence program of $2 billion a year to face. Our federal and provincial government social security expenses now are $1,500 million and of that $1,500 million the federal government is responsible for 80 per cent.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Now what are we charged with today in this country, in this house? We are charged with having overtaxed the people of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. gentlemen say "hear, hear", tout that is the charge. Our answer to that is that while it is true we have the highest tax load ever experienced in peacetime, it is because we have embarked upon a defence program as well as maintaining the other normal functions of peacetime government. We have at the same time, in the light of our capacity as we see it, embarked upon important social security and health programs.
What would a health insurance program cost? My hon. friend said $400 million. A health insurance program in this country would cost much more than that. Such a program in this country would have to face the matter of additional costs of all kinds; and what the government has to consider is whether, in the light of our tremendous financial commitments for defence and all our peacetime activities, we could meet the additional burden that would be imposed upon us. It is all very well to talk about this sort of thing and to say just do it, but we can only do it in one way; that is by imposing an additional financial burden on the people who have to pay for it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The money for all these schemes-for old age pensions, for family allowances, and for all these' things-comes from but one source, and that is the hard work of the Canadian people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
They are carrying a big load now. We think it is a load that is within the capacity of this nation; to go ahead without consideration from the provinces, without consideration of their attitude, I suggest would be not only unwise; not only would it have the elements of irresponsibility, but it would have the elements of danger, so much so that the scheme itself might not succeed.
I believe the national health program we have undertaken in this country in collaboration with the provinces is a necessary groundwork. I am asked to declare now when such a scheme is to be adopted. Of course in keeping with the traditions of responsible government that is the prerogative, as it must be, of governments themselves. Whatever the policy of the government may be in the light of the continuing situation, that is a matter which the government will announce on its responsibility when it thinks the appropriate moment has


come. When will that be? Well, many hon. members have been suggesting that we have been making all sorts of studies. Of course we have been making studies. A few years ago we were charged with not making any. While we have not been criticized for-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The charge bore fruit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have no better authority for the decision on the present course than the words of the hon. member who has just interjected. This afternoon he said, and I fully agree with him on this, that the house is well aware how anxious some of us are to get a health insurance program established, but it is equally important that it become established on a proper basis. In my judgment the hon. gentleman never uttered truer words.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think the minister should give the rest of the quotation. I stand by the words, but I was referring to one plan as contrasted with another.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
If that was the case I accept what my hon. friend has said, but juist as the words of a good man are applicable to any situation, so are his words in this particular context.
This program upon which we have embarked is important. The work of building hospitals, providing medical research, providing for cancer control and t.b. control, providing for improvement in mental health -those are very important efforts and are a very important basis for what might follow. It is a program that has won, I am happy to say, the complete co-operation of the ten provincial governments. It is one of which this country can be justifiably proud.
I conclude what I have to say by mentioning what I said a few minutes ago, when I was asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre whether we were going to establish a health insurance committee. I told him then, as I tell him now, that all the provincial health surveys are not in. Not one of them has yet been fully assessed by the provincial governments or by ourselves. These surveys are going to take a good deal of honest digging, in which we are now engaged. On top of that is the fact that the most important-as I said last night, on the authority of the American public health association-morbidity and sickness survey ever undertaken in any jurisdiction is the one we started about two years ago under this program. Using 40,000 individual cases, we are seeking to estimate medical care costs and hospital care costs as they apply to individuals, as they apply

to families and as they apply to local communities. This survey is just about complete, and we are going to assess that. When we have made these assessments the government will be in a position, in the light of the over-all obligations that it has with provincial governments, and with many other problems, to decide the next step.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is good to know that the minister, speaking for the government, has not gone back on the promise some day to establish health insurance in Canada. It is good to know that some day there is to be an announcement of the next step. But, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the excellent case which the minister may feel he has made for delay in this matter, that is all it amounts to, simply delay and delay. He cannot turn aside the fact that this subject has been studied by his party for 33 years, and very actively for the past 10 or 12 years.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the evidence the minister piles up concerning the amount of study and research that has been conducted only demonstrates that we should have had that special health insurance committee at this session. In fact the more the minister makes it clear that his department is possessed of a mass of material, the more tragic I feel it is that that committee was not appointed. I would hope that had the committee been appointed it might have gone a long way toward making recommendations to parliament. But even if it had not been able to wade through the mass of material the department laid before it, and thus reach the point of making recommendations, at least it would have been an education for the members of the committee, for members of parliament generally and for the public to have that material laid before the committee, studied, digested and given to the public generally. I am still not satisfied with the answers that have been given as to why this change was made.
Last June we were certainly given the impression that we were to have a committee at this session. Last fall when we were down here we were certainly under the impression that when we came back for the 1952 session, we would have a health insurance committee. As a matter of fact, when I left home in February to come to this session it was still very much in the news that one of the most important matters before parliament at this session would be the special committee on health insurance. It was only after I arrived in Ottawa the morning the session opened or the day before, I forget which, that one of my friends told me he had seen a rumour in the newspapers that the health insurance committee had been called off. A decision made in that way, so suddenly, I suggest was
Supply-Health and Welfare not only a disappointment-I think to the minister too-but a tragedy for the people of Canada.
I believe the minister protests too much in the effort he makes to explain why we must wait still longer before the next step is taken.
I agree with his statement that any health insurance plan must be well founded. He knows that when I made that statement this afternoon, I was making it in reference to the kind of plan to which the member for Broadview had referred and the kind of plan to which the member for Eglinton had referred. I was making it clear that I wanted a plan that would provide health insurance not just for the healthy and the wealthy but for the entire community. Indeed, one very excellent way to get that health insurance plan well founded would have been to have a committee dealing with this matter and getting information on this question out to the public. We have lost that chance for that type of educational work, for that kind of ground work, at this session. I repeat that, in my view, it is a tragedy.
Tonight the minister used the words the Minister of National Revenue used last evening: what about the cost? The minister picked up the figure I gave of $400 million, and said that a health insurance program would cost a great deal more than that. He has not yet given a figure. "A great deal more than that" he says, and that might be another $100 million or a total of $500 million. When I gave that figure of $400 million last night I gave it as a figure representing approximately the amount of money Canadians are now spending on health and hospital care. I arrived at that figure by adding together certain figures in one of the sessional papers the minister had tabled.
I reminded the Minister of National Revenue last night, as I now wish to remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare, of what was said in the report of the committee on old age security with respect to this very question, namely the cost of a health insurance program. I quote now from page 104 of that report:
It has been estimated however that the over-all cost of a comprehensive system of health insurance would probably be not less than $300 million annually-
I have been prepared to accept a higher figure.
-although it must be added that a large-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Twice that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
All right; twice as much, if you will. I suggest to the minister, while I am interrupting this quotation, that it is not a case of whether we can afford to have health insurance; we cannot afford not to

Supply-Health and Welfare have it. The minister knows that view was expressed clearly in a document to which I drew his attention before. Then, to go on with the quotation:
-although it must be added that a large proportion of such an amount would represent not a new burden on the people of Canada, but merely a rechannelling of existing expenditures on various forms of health care.
Now, I do not wish to oversimplify the matter. I do not wish to get away from the fact that when we have a health insurance program we will be spending more on health than the total amount we are spending now. Once we have a health insurance program many forms of health care people are not getting now will be made available to them. Indeed that is one of the reasons for having a national health insurance program. But the minister should not give the impression that whatever figure he gives, be it $400 million or $500 million or $600 million, is a new sum of money the whole of which will have to be found. A large portion of it, perhaps half or three-quarters, will simply be a rechannelling of money that is now being spent on health care by the people of Canada in one form or another.
The minister has indicated that a great deal of study has been given to the matter. We have these various recommendations, and it does seem to me that he should go a bit further than he did tonight. He should give the House of Commons the assurance that an early opportunity will be provided for a committee to study all this material, and get moving on a health insurance program.
He does not like us to use that language. He does not like us to say, "Get moving; get going." Well, what does he want to do? Does he want just to sit and wait? We have to get moving somewhere, somehow, and the experience we have had with old age pensions bears out the validity of the position the minister took last year, that it would be a good idea to have a committee of this kind.
The minister spent a good deal of time just now, in the earlier part of his remarks at any rate, in criticizing the plan in existence in Sweden at the present time, and in that part of his speech he disagreed with the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview. But he did not comment on the plan proposed by the new legislation in Sweden. He gave his opinion as to why it is not yet in effect, but he did not say whether he favoured the new plan as against the old one. I certainly do.
He did not comment on the plan in Denmark. He did not comment on the plans in Great Britain or in New Zealand, which have been studied by his department through

the provision of the money we are now voting. I feel we are entitled to some further statement from him as to the type of health insurance plan he and his officials feel would be good for Canada, in the light of studies that have been made under this very note.
I feel, too, that the minister should face up to the fact that old age pensions in the first place were brought in before all the provinces were ready to participate. Indeed Mr. King made it clear, once he had been put in the position where he had to bring in old age pensions, that he was not going to delay the bill because some provinces did not want to come ini He made it clear that since the measure was a good one, and since some provinces were ready to participate, they should be given that opportunity.
As I have already said, the Saskatchewan health survey report recommends that the same policy be pursued with respect to health insurance. Let me read again paragraph 5 of its recommendations as they appear at page 226 of the report. It says:
In the event It is decided that health insurance is to be organized and administered1 on a provincial rather than on a national level, the federal government should adopt immediately the provisions for a national health insurance program as contained in the proposals to the provinces in 1945.
May I interject to point out that because this comes from Saskatchewan it does not follow that it has any particular political flavour. It does not come from the provincial government of that province; it comes from a health survey committee consisting of very eminent people in the field of public health, appointed under the direction of the present minister. It will be noted that this committee recommends that we should have immediate adoption at the federal level of a national health insurance program as contained in the proposals made to the provinces in 1945 by this very federal government. I go on with the quotation:
The federal government should establish basic standards to be met by the provinces as conditions for receiving the grants in order to provide at least minimum uniform benefits throughout all Canada, with reciprocity of benefits for insured persons moving from one province to another.
I feel that while we are on this item, in which we are asked to vote money for health insurance studies, the minister should tell us something further about what he thinks of the new proposal in Sweden, what he thinks of the plan in New Zealand, what he thinks of the plan in Great Britain, and what he thinks about this recommendation made by the Saskatchewan health survey committee for the immediate establishment of a nation-wide health insurance plan with

a provision for provincial participation. All the evidence makes it clear that the time has come for action on this very important question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When the minister was tearing down this Swedish plan, which has been in successful operation for 25 years, he made *a point of playing with figures. He said there were no children insured under the plan, and that only 50 per cent of the people in Sweden participated.
I wish to refer to page 6 of his own memorandum, and to quote therefrom:
In 1933 there were just under one million members, but in 1949-
And this shows the natural healthy growth of a plan which is successful.
-this had risen to nearly three million adult members, with over 1-23 million children covered for medical benefits through some 1,100 funds; this coverage represented approximately 60 per cent of the total population.
There is an awful lot of difference between one and a quarter million and no children, as the minister claims. There is a lot of difference between his claim of 50 per cent, and the 60 per cent which is the actual figure of coverage today. It seems to me too bad that when he tries to tear down a plan which has been successful in another country, he cannot use correct figures when taking part in the discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the item covering civil defence. I shall not at this time go into the arguments or remarks that I have advanced at various times during the past three or four years to indicate the extreme importance of civil defence. The fact that the government has finally realized that it is really a matter of some importance is indicated by the fact that some $4 million odd was appropriated last year and that figure is up this year by better than $2 million.
Although $4,196,202 was appropriated for this last year, in the list the minister gave yesterday of expenditures of his department, which appears at page 2967 of Hansard, I see that expenditures on civil defence are listed as being only $844,851. I would like to ask how those two figures are reconciled. It would appear from these figures that $4 million odd was appropriated but only $800,000 was spent on this extremely important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows the estimate was higher than the amount actually spent. I think the house would generally agree that it is very fortunate that we have not had to spend more. I have had to make an assessment of the situation as we see it, in the light of the international situation and in the light of the action the provinces themselves are prepared to take. There were other factors, such as the difficulty of getting certain kinds of equipment.
What the situation will be this year, in the light of our assessment, I do not know. We

have budgeted, as my hon. friend has said, for a higher figure. We have also incorporated into that a provision which extends the proposed direction that the federal government has been willing to give in this matter. Instead of providing only for equipment, training material, training schools, paying expenses of trained personnel, directors and so on, we are going to extend by entering into a matching arrangement with the provinces, and we will be prepared then to entertain, on a fifty-fifty basis, any project which they feel should be undertaken in this field over and above what we have heretofore done.
I am sure the house will remember that we recently had a visit to Canada by the director general of civil defence training in the United Kingdom, Sir John Hodsoll, who perhaps has had more experience in civil defence than any other individual in the world, certainly in the western world. He has visited us several times, and our officers have visited him. We have modelled our civil defence organization pretty well along the lines that he established in England both during and after world war II. His contributions to us have been very helpful, and I would remind the house of the statement he made in London the other day when commenting on his visit to Canada and the United States. I quote from the Montreal Star of May 9:
Canada Tops U.S. in Civil Defence
Sir John Hodsoll, Britain's number one expert on the subject, said today he rates Canada ahead of the United States in civil defence. Back from a visit to Canada, where he watched a rehearsal of defence services, Sir John said much progress has been made in the last couple of years.
That is in Canada.
"They are rapidly catching up on our own organization," said the head of Britain's civil defence services. "The Americans on the other hand are more apathetic."
He said he hopes to see an exchange system for civil defence instruction arranged between Canada and the U.S.
I merely mention that as an indication of his general concurrence with the lines we have taken. I may say that at the recent conference we had with the provincial governments here we were able to arrive at a very considerable measure of agreement, and the general opinion was that in our combined efforts we were proceeding along sensible lines, building up the basis of an adequate civil defence organization not in its ultimate terms but in those terms which, in the light of circumstances as we see them, are practicable and necessary at this time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I must say that the first part of the minister's remarks are quite amazing to me. I just do not think they make sense. Last year we voted $4,196,202, and I would take from the minister's remarks that $844,000

was the actual amount spent. Then he says that this year everybody in Canada should appreciate the fact that we did not have to spend more. He commented on the international situation and apparently indicated that it was not necessary to spend more than the $844,000. But even this year the sum of $6 * 5 million is appropriated, and only about $2 million was spent. The two things do not jibe. We have been told by the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others that the international situation has improved during the past year. In the light of those statements the earlier part of the minister's remarks just do not make sense. If his defence for spending so little is correct, then there should not be as much as this appropriated for this year. If the amount appropriated for this year is required, then the amount that was estimated would be required for last year indicates that something is wrong in the way this matter has been handled.
I believe the minister stated he was sure everyone in Canada would appreciate that there had not been a greater expenditure than there has been. Personally I do not appreciate that fact at all. I think the money should have been spent; not only that amount, but that probably considerably more could have been profitably spent. I believe the fact that such a small amount was spent really indicates a lack of energy and a lack of leadership so far as the minister and his department are concerned in carrying out this phase of their work. I believe that instead of being applauded for saving money they should be censured for having done so little. The minister quoted certain remarks made by the British civil defence head following his visit to Canada. I do not think those remarks could be taken as an endorsement of what the minister has done, or perhaps I should say what he has not done. I believe it creates quite a wrong impression to quote those words.
To touch on a specific question, last year we had quite a long discussion on this matter, and at that time the subject of the discussion was the standardization of hose couplings across Canada. Part of the money that was voted was to be used to assist the municipalities in carrying out this hose standardization program. I should like to ask the minister how far that standardization program has gone, how much assistance was given, and how much remains to be accomplished.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I noticed what the hon. member said earlier about the lack of leadership, and that is his opinion. I put his opinion against that of Sir John Hodsoll. I am in the
Supply-Health and Welfare unusual position tonight of being criticized for not spending money. I am sure the country will be interested in that observation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am sure they will, too.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The reason a lot of this money was not spent, apart from the reasons I have already indicated, was that some of this program was predicated upon a matching arrangement with the provinces. The standardization of hose couplings is one such example; that is an arrangement which depends upon corresponding action by the provinces. The provinces of Ontario and Alberta are the only ones which, within the past few months, have agreed to take advantage of this matching offer. If they had come earlier or if the other provinces had come last year, the whole amount would have been spent. For one reason or another they did not come. These two provinces have done so, and that will represent an increased expenditure. If they had come last year there would have been another $900,000 spent. Unfortunately we could not get agreement with them until within the last few months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister still has not said how much was used for the standardization of hose couplings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I just said that last year there was none. We have entered into an agreement with the provinces of Alberta and Ontario. Pursuant to that arrangement Ontario will receive I think about $300,000 and the province of Alberta will receive one-third of the cost of their program.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is a little difficult to get an answer from the minister which can be readily understood. He has said that these agreements have been entered into, which would naturally lead one to believe that if they had been entered into some of last year's appropriation would have been used. Apparently they were not entered into until last year's vote had lapsed; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, we only entered into the agreements with both these provinces since January 1 of this year. We were ready to do so last spring.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It still seems to me there has been something lacking in getting this done. I do not know that all the blame can be thrown on the provinces for the fact the agreements had not been entered into.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I was not blaming anyone; I was simply stating the facts.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That was the way I understood it.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am sorry, but I cannot give you understanding.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It was the minister's suggestion as to why this vote had not been used. I should like to ask what progress has been made in regard to other equipment about which we heard a good deal last year. I remember there was quite a bit of talk about the provision of small wireless sets for communication purposes, which were going to be provided by the dominion government. As I remember, there was a provision for steel helmets and certain first-aid supplies. Can the minister tell us what has been done with regard to that equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am going to give the hon. member the picture in its entirety. I think perhaps that would be the best way to do it. The increase in this year's estimates reflects a development which has taken place in our program since the fall of 1950, when that year's estimates were prepared by the Department of National Defence. At that time the program was in its earliest stages, and it was impossible for the Department of National Defence to forecast accurately the trends the rate of development and the financial requirements to meet them. Sixty-five per cent, or an increase of $1,400,000, is to cover the provision of grants to the provinces for general civil defence purposes. Last year no such provision was made. It is proposed to offer to assist the provinces in meeting the cost of administration and the purchase of operational requirements for civil defence purposes by per capita grants on the following basis: target area populations will get 14 cents per capita and the non-target areas 8 cents per capita. These grants, as such, will be on a matching basis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What does the minister mean "on a matching basis"?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We will pay 50 per cent. Take the hon. member's own city of Vancouver, where they are concerned about the question ,of a communications control centre. There is some discussion between the province and the city concerning the financial responsibility for that particular item. If the province of British Columbia submits to us a project in respect of the building of a civil defence communications control centre in Vancouver, we would be prepared to give consideration to paying 50 per cent of the cost of that item; that is the way we would deal with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The province is to pay the other half?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The province or the province and the municipality combined, but we would insist that some contribution be made by the


province itself whether it was the full 50 per cent or a portion of the 50 per cent. We would only pay 50 per cent of the cost of the project.
The second largest increase, $624,000, was for materials and supplies, and by far the largest item is $2,100,000 for stockpiling medical supplies. This is a program under which we are engaged in the stockpiling of medical supplies at a cost this year of $12,100,000. Those supplies will be stationed ait strategic areas or existing national defence depots. There will be no loss in the event of non-use of these medical supplies that will be so stockpiled. If they are not used-and we trust they will never be needed-for purposes of war disaster, then 90 per cent of them can be used for the normal purposes of our own department or the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Then with regard to perishable items such as penicillin, we have made arrangements with the drug houses for the storage of these in their own specially equipped warehouses. There is no financial commitment involved, except the assurance by them that supplies will be available in accordance with the program.
We have increased our educational information and materials program by $166,000 to meet requests of the provinces for films, manuals and so on.
An item of $90,000 is being provided for the lease of communications services. That is a communication system for the country as a whole. The attack warning system will cost $40,000, and the attack warning system extension another $40,000. The control system for broadcast services will be roughly $10,000.
There is likewise an increase of $80,000 for travelling expenses other than staff. These are to pay for expenses of individuals sent to us by the provinces and the municipalities, who go to our training centre at Ottawa for training. We pay their travelling and living expenses.
Then another $80,000 is being provided to subsidize the St. John ambulance organization. They are engaged in the process of providing first-aid training of individuals, apart from their normal complement.
Then we will have 32 per cent of this item or roughly $2,089,000, for the acquisition of equipment such as self-propelled fire pumps; our share of the cost in the standardization of hose couplings; radiation detection systems; stirrup pumps; additional sirens; 10 rescue vehicles for the distribution to the provinces for training purposes, respirators and the like.
Then to follow up the question of the hon. member, last year we provided 65,000 helmets

to the provinces, and through them to the municipalities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is that all that was provided in the way of equipment lined up last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh, no; we provided stretchers, blankets and gas respirators; we have provided manuals, films, instructors, and we have trained individuals. The total expenditures involved in civil defence are not to be calculated merely by this $845,000, because a lot of the work that goes into educational material, and so on, is the normal work that is carried on by the department itself, and includes the use of the staff. If we were, for instance, to calculate the work of the defence research board it would run into many millions of dollars. But I suspect that the way to judge the adequacy of civil defence is not merely by the expenditure of money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, no one is suggesting that the civil defence program is to be judged solely on the expenditure of money. Nevertheless the situation is that last year we were given a considerable number of items by the minister when he pointed out all these things they were going to do with the $4 million voted at that time. It is rather shocking to find now that a total expenditure of only $800,000 was made, and that most of the things the minister said were going to be done last year were not done. He has just given us another statement of what will be done in the coming year, and it leads one to suspect that the same thing will happen again.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will say this, that I will not authorize- the expenditure of any more money than the provinces and ourselves deem necessary. And I should think that would be in harmony with the policy the opposition has been urging for the last few months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that may sound like a very nice statement by the minister; but I happen to know that at least one province thinks a considerably larger amount is necessary than has thus far been authorized by the minister or his department. That is the province from which I come. The chief complaint I hear out there in regard to civil defence is the difficulty of getting the dominion government to provide funds or equipment, or to make any definite arrangement for damage that may arise. That is the sort of problem that is holding up the full operation of an efficient civil defence plan. So what the minister just said does not apply in that province. I do not know whether it applies in other provinces or not.
In any event it seems to me that if we are going to make progress in civil defence in
Supply-Health and Welfare this country, then the government which has to take the lead is the dominion government. So far as I have been able to see in connection with this civil defence matter, right from its inception one of the greatest difficulties in so far as making progress is concerned has been the uncertainty of the sphere of responsibility of the dominion, provincial and municipal governments. As a result there has been a great deal of what one might describe as buck-passing. In many cases one government thinks some other government should be doing this, that or the other thing. It seems to me there has not yet been a sufficiently clear delimitation of the respective responsibilities, or what agreements may be made with respect to those responsibilities. That is one of the things I believe are responsible for holding up the civil defence plan at the present time.
One of the things, for example, that I know cause difficulty is making payments to persons who are injured in the course of civil defence duties. If this is not so, then I hope the minister will correct me, and say what the situation is. So far as I know no definite arrangement has yet been made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, there is.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
So far as I know no definite arrangement has been made as to who will pay for property damage which may be caused through, we will say, civil defence exercises, or from an actual raid. No decision has been made so far as I know as to who will pay for injuries caused to persons, or who will compensate them for the time they lose from their work.
For instance, I know that if reserve army personnel are on military exercises and while on those exercises are injured, they are hospitalized in a military hospital and receive pay and allowances during the time they are in hospital. But so far as I know there is no provision along that line for civil defence personnel. In the same way the government has a responsibility for property damage caused through army exercises, and generally without much question it pays the damage.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are compensation agreements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister has been attempting to say something for some time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, I have been trying to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then would he tell us exactly what the provisions are in regard to these two matters, namely property damage and compensation to civilian personnel suffering injury?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
With regard to property
damage there is no agreement. The provinces
3022	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare and ourselves thought the time had not come; and there is no such agreement in any country in the western world. Then with regard to compensation to civil defence workers, the situation now is that during 1951-52 a policy was established whereby the federal government would pay 50 per cent of costs incurred for compensation purposes under workmen's compensation acts for persons injured undergoing civil defence training. We anticipate that during the present fiscal year we will have an agreement signed with all the provinces. We discussed that at the recent conference and there was general satisfaction with the agreement. I think the one with Ontario is practically complete in all its terms. Provisions for compensation for civil defence workers are now under way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not know whether I understand what the minister means. He said that compensation was going to be paid under the workmen's compensation boards of the various provinces, did he?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are using the machinery of the workmen's compensation boards, and we will undertake to pay 50 per cent of the cost involved.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What I would understand by that is that a person who is in the civil defence organization and is injured in the course of his duties will receive compensation at the rate laid down by the provincial compensation board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Which will mean, so far as the average man is concerned, certainly the man in what you might call business or professional life, that he will be receiving compensation, if he is laid up in hospital for two or three months, we will say, as a result of injury received, at the rate of approximately $20 a week, or something along that line.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It would depend on the rates of the workmen's compensation board. That was the proposal of the provinces and we concurred in that, and I think it is a very satisfactory arrangement. It is the arrangement they have in the United States, too, by the way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I find myself very perplexed about this question. I want to ask the minister one or two questions, not on points pf detail but on the broad situation. Are the people of Canada really taking this thing seriously? When I ask that question I begin to ask it of myself and I have the answer, I think; that I have not taken it very seriously, and I am not quite sure whom to blame for that. It seems to me 

that we either take it seriously or we do not. Now, translating it into the matter of expenditure, the minister had it pointed out to him that only a fraction of what was appropriated last year was spent, and he said: "Are you not glad we did not spend the money?" In one sense of course we are glad to save money; but surely it raises the question whether or not we are taking this seriously.
Secondly, when the minister was asked about the estimate appropriated for next year I think his words were: "We will not spend anything more than the dominion and the provinces think is sensible." All right, I agree with that; but that again does not answer my question. The minister knows what was spent last year. He knows, for example, whether it has been accelerating. He must have some amounts in mind as to what we are to spend this year as against last year. I should like to know something about that. But more than that, and to my way of thinking much more important, are we really taking this thing seriously?
The minister quoted an official from England who was here, and who no doubt is a distinguished person whose views are entitled to whatever weight they should receive, but we do know that people who come visiting officials, if they are wise, do not say anything critical about the country they are in, and they find it much easier to say things that are pleasant. Therefore I come back again to this, Mr. Chairman. This thing either is important or it is not. If it is important, it seems to me we are not taking it very seriously. If it is not important, let us face the facts. Will the minister answer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will do it now. This matter is important. There can be no question of doubt about the importance of civil defence. When the estimates were before this house last year we had about 9,000 civil defence workers in Canada. Today we have over 62,000. In England they have but 200,000 civil defence workers actually enrolled. The city of Winnipeg, for instance, has more than 3,500 civil defence workers. The budget for civil defence in the city of Montreal is over $200,000 a year. I just mention these instances now to show that we are taking this matter seriously. We have a training school here in Ottawa. We have trained over 1,200 individuals in the last year and a half.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What do
they do?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They go back and act as civil defence directors and instructors in their own communities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Why have they not been to see me?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Some of them have been to see you. You and I had lunch with them, with no less than Sir John Hodsoll himself, and he was the one who told you-this was a social engagement, and I should not bring that in. But we had an adequate discussion. I brought the hon. member in there because I did feel that perhaps he was not taking this as seriously as I thought he should. I am glad to know that the hon. member is interested.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I want to know who the man is in my district. He has not been to see me.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh, well-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not know what I am to do when I get a bomb on my house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is not in his constituency sufficiently long for the man to see him. Mr. Welsh, the provincial secretary of Ontario, is in charge of the civil defence of Ontario. Air Vice-Marshal Lawrence is the civil defence director in the city of Toronto, and he has his staff. I am sure that under his capable administration the hon. member's district is being taken care of. I could find out in five minutes who the individual is and tell the hon. member who should call on hirh when he is next in his constituency.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If he says he has been to see me I say he has not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is an extremely difficult problem. One has to take into account the possibility of immediate use, and the possibility of non-use for a long time. You can build an organization up away beyond capacity and have it suddenly fall. The expenditure that would be involved would be great and the resulting loss of morale and so on would be very considerable. My hon. friend may be assured that the appropriations that we are dealing with here represent the joint consideration of the provinces and ourselves, of what at this time we shall endeavour to do; and if equipment is available we shall be able to say next year, provided that the situation continues as we see it, that most of this money has been expended. That will depend on contingencies, however, that I cannot foresee. But my hon. friend may be assured that this matter is an important one and that the provinces, the municipalities and ourselves are so regarding it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The minister spoke a moment ago about the danger of the loss of 55704-191
Supply-Health and Welfare morale through moving too quickly and then having things sort of peter out. So far as morale is concerned, I think the difficulty he is confronted with at the present time is just the opposite. It is that he is not moving nearly fast enough to keep up the morale of the people who have come forward up to date and been taking part in this civil defence work. Most of the people I know, at any rate, who have been taking an interest in this matter and have been trying to get something going in connection with it are now feeling full of frustration because of the fact that the equipment they thought they were going to get under the various arrangements they were making has not been forthcoming. To that extent they feel that they have been butting their heads against a very hard surface of some sort. If there is going to be any talk of morale then I think of the morale of those people who have come forward and given up their time in order to try to build this civil defence organization into something which will be efficient. Certainly I think their morale is suffering.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Alberta is one of the best provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister indicate the extent of the organization in the city of London?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes. I am sure my hon. friend knows Eric Harris who is in charge of the civil defence organization in that district. Under him there has been developed a network of organizations in the various municipalities. The province reports to us that that organization is working well; that it is doing an excellent job indeed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am glad to hear the minister say that because I had some contact with them, and I was under the impression that probably they were the best organization in Ontario, if not in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Very good.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have some questions to ask, and since it is eleven will you let this item stand?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Ask them now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
You do not want to ask them
now?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No, I would rather not.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
